speakeroldname: Hon. C. W. G. GIBSON (Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: INCOME TAX
subtopic: POSTPONEMENT UNTIL AUGUST 31 OP BALANCE OWING ON QUARTERLY INSTALMENT BASIS
speechtext:
I should like to clarify the previous statement I made on March 27 concerning the extension of time for the payment of income tax by individuals. Strictly interpreted the statement would exclude those taxpayers who pay their taxes on the quarterly 
instalment plan. I should like to make it clear that taxpayers who have estimated their tax on a quarterly instalment basis, as required by the Income War Tax Act, will be granted until August 31 to pay, without interest, any additional tax that may be owing over and above what was estimated.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, March 7, consideration in committee of the report of the special committee on the revision of standing orders, Mr. Bradette in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
The first amendment proposed is to standing order 9, which at present reads as follows:
Upon a division, the yeas and nays shall not be entered upon the minutes, unless demanded by five members.
The amendment proposed is as follows:
And every member present in the chamber when the question is finally put by Mr. Speaker shall be obliged to vote, and if he does not vote Mr. Speaker shall call upon him to vote and his name shall be recorded accordingly. - If he persists in not voting he may be named by Mr. Speaker for having violated a standing order of the house.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether the procedure you are now adopting is that which was agreed upon unanimously at a previous sitting, when this report was discussed. But it would appear that this procedure would bar any general discussion with respect to this matter, and I rather fancy one or two hon. members in any event would wish to make some general observations before going into the more limited discussion on the amendments to the various standing orders.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a very short comment upon what has been said in this matter. I believe the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Pouliot) is somewhat beside the point when he refers to the first part of the report as being a preamble. It is not a preamble, except in a very general sense. Certainly it is not a preamble such as one finds at the beginning of a bill.
But the hon. member is quite correct in his statement that when a committee of this kind reports it thereupon ceases to exist. That will be found in paragraph 664 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, which states:
If a committee at the conclusion of their inquiry, make a final report to the fiouse, the sittings of the committee are assumed to have been closed, and if further proceedings were desired, it would be necessary to revive the committee.
That does not matter so much at the moment, except that I believe Mr. Speaker . told us the last time the matter was discussed that the committee might further consider the matter and make further representations. That, of course, would be impossible under the circumstances.
The leader of the opposition raised a further point of order. He said that some members might wish to speak on the general aspect of the report. I would also point out that in the earlier part of the report-which the chairman appears to have ignored, because he begins in the middle of it, at page 4-recommendations
are made. What are we going to do with them?
I say that there is a definite recommendation by the committee, which reads as follows:
We therefore recommend that, when the yearly estimates have been brought down, one day a week be set aside for consideration of supply.
Then there is the further definite recommendation :
Our recommendation is that, when there is reason to believe that debate will be protracted, parties and groups recognized in the house shall confer and make arrangements-[DOT]
And so on. It provides that groups shall get together and do something about it, a procedure which I submit is quite illegal.
There are two definite recommendations. What are we going to do about them? Because, the amendments to the standing orders having been considered, I presume the thing will conclude. Or are we to go backwards and begin again? Would it not be better to do as the leader of the opposition has suggested, namely, begin at the beginning and deal with all the recommendations, after having a general debate? The debate was by no means concluded when the matter was up some time ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, might I say a word for purposes of expedition. It will be noted that on March 7 Mr. Speaker closed the debate, as it appears at page 1262 of Hansard, with these words:
I therefore suggest that the committee report progress and ask leave to sit again on another day when, if the committee so desires, we may deal with the amendments which are printed on pages 149 to 152 of Votes and Proceedings.
I am suggesting that if we make the progress which I am assuming we would make in connection with the specific amendments to the rules of the house, we should vote upon them as soon as we can. We can give some indication as to whether we are against them or in favour of them, and have some action in the matter.
Ten specific recommendations are made by the committee. I believe the committee was unanimous in respect of most of them. But on the other hand I do not think it would insist upon any if the house were against them. In my view the essential procedure this afternoon is to find out upon what the house agrees, and to do it with all possible expedition. I do not think debate will help us much in regard to these specific recommendations. I suggest we leave the generalizations and the introductory features mentioned, so that we may deal with the specific amendments suggested by the committee.
Rules of the House

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: May I speak again on a point of order? In my view it would be unfortunate if this debate were to be extended to any great length.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I cannot hear the leader of the opposition.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I am not disagreeing with my hon. friend. I try to speak as loudly as I can on these occasions, so that he will be able to hear. I agree to this extent with the Minister of Pensions and National Health, that perhaps it would be unwise, unless there is some special reason for so doing, to have an extended general debate in the matter. Nevertheless there are a number of members who, if the procedure were directed along more restricted channels, would be deprived of an opportunity to speak. Some hon. members who spoke on the earlier occasion had the advantage of speaking generally, and if the debate were restricted I believe those of us who perhaps now have something to say along general lines would suffer an injustice. I think it would be unfair to make, that restriction, even at the expense of extending the debate a little longer than might normally be required.
When Mr. Speaker on the earlier occasion made his observations at the conclusion of that sitting, I do not think he had in mind any curtailment of the rights of those who might wish to speak in a general way, and in respect of the general aspects of the matter.
The report dealt not only with specific matters affecting changes in the rules, but it went on in some detail to philosophize somewhat in respect of rules generally, and house deportment. It is my belief that we would make just as much headway, and perhaps in the end save considerable time, if hon. members were given leeway in the same manner as obtained on the earlier occasion. I have always felt that when there is an attempt-I am not saying any such attempt is being made on this occasion-to curtail general discussion in the house it takes longer than if we proceed in the regular way. If hon. members have something to say we might as well allow them to have their say at this time. It is my suggestion, in order that the matter may be clarified, that we go on with the general discussion, beginning where we left off on the earlier occasion. Then, having finished that, we could get down to the particular items. I fancy it would not take quite so long then to deal with those items.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: How shall we determine when that debate is finished?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
When I spoke at the last sitting of the committee in connection with the rules' 
I did not intend there'should be any limitation of discussion on the part of any hon. member of the committee. I was concerned, of course, principally with the passing of the amendments that will have to be discussed. The hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) speaks of this as a preamble. It is not a preamble; it is simply the bases upon which the committee is being asked to pass amendments to the rules. When the amendments to the rules are being discussed there is nothing to prevent any hon. member of the committee from referring to what is a commentary on the reasons why the amendments were being asked for. But in view of the attitude of the hon. members who have spoken, which I think is the mind of the hon. members of the committee, I should be willing and agree that there should be the general discussion to which the leader of the opposition has referred. But I would point out that we are still on the first portion of the report, which is, if I may say so, the historical part of the reasons for the amendments. The matters before the committee, after all, are the amendments of the rules. That is the question for the committee. It is a matter wholly within the hands of the committee. Our committee have met and have reported. It is now within the judgment of the committee of the whole whether these few rules shall be amended or not. In so far as the committee is concerned it is entirely in the hands of the committee of the whole, which is now sitting.	.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
After listening this noon to the finest music and the most harmonious melodies coming from the tower of the 'parliament buildings, it is painful to be confronted in this chamber with a report submitted for the purpose of restricting some of the most important rights, privileges and liberties of the people's representatives in parliament.
I would have no objection to most of the amendments submitted in this report. For the moment I shall not state any objection I may have to the amendments to standing orders 9, 12, 31, 37, 40, 43 and 44; but I am strongly opposed to the proposed amendment to standing order 49. This amendment completely contradicts the principles set forth in the presentation or preamble, if we can call it that, which appears in the report of the special committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I would ask the hon. member to speak to the point of order raised by the leader of the opposition. We are discussing the point of order at the present time.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I believe we should go on with the fullest, frankest and freest dis-

Rules of the House
cussion of this whole matter. Parliament is the place where the people's representatives meet to talk. While the committee which considered the matter had a good chance to go into all the aspects of the proposed changes, a large number of the members of parliament have not had such an opportunity. I believe it will be altogether beneficial to have a complete discussion in this committee, even if it takes us a day or two. Let us remember that the rules as they stand to-day are the result of the experience of our forefathers over hundreds of years. We cannot afford lightly to change them. We should give most careful consideration to every proposed change. I therefore favour allowing complete, frank and general discussion before we proceed with the items.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I believe the point raised is either to call for a general or a clause by clause discussion of this report. There is one point I should like to point out. I think it would save time if we took up the report as a whole first and then considered the list of very moderate changes. The reference to the committee called for a revision of the standing orders of the house. It was a broad resolution and gave the committee the power to go much farther than they have gone. I refer to one matter that does not appear in the list, rule 9. In the British House of Commons under their rule 9 private members and all the members may question the government, ask questions which are not on the order paper, up to a quarter to four. They can practically cross-examine the ministers on any questions of urgent public importance. What is our rule? We have to move on an urgent matter the adjournment of the house and get twenty members to stand up. One may wish to question the government on one of the most important emergency questions that could arise, but unless one gets the support of twenty members one cannot do it. Take a question like housing. I could not ask a question on it to-day under our rules without moving the adjournment of the house and having twenty members stand. Even then the Speaker automatically has the power to say whether in his opinion it is an urgent matter. That I think is unwise. I suggest that general discussion take place first.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
We have been discussing the questions asked by the leader of the opposition. The hon. member for Temiscouata mentioned a preamble. I think that has been answered. There is no preamble, only an introduction. I believe I know the consensus of the committee. I believe hon. members want a general discussion. It is recognized that this is not an ordinary measure. I believe 100-147
it would be in order to allow a general discussion. There is no possibility of amendments as far as the introduction is concerned, but there is a possibility of amendments when the proposed amendments are brought before the committee for discussion.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Before we begin the general discussion, may we have some definite ruling from the Chair? After all, what we are dealing with here is a report of a special committee. Is the Chair proposing that we shall first of all have a general discussion and then consider the report section by section? If we have the general discussion, would amendments then be in order? Will there be a vote on the report as a whole? These amendments are not a series of proposals; they are brought down as one proposal as a report of the committee. I should like the Chair to make that clear; otherwise we may do a lot of rambling.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I agree with the hon. member who has just spoken. I think there are ten distinct amendments. Each one is separate and each one should be dealt with separately. We should take the judgment of the committee as a whole on each one, and either reject it or adopt it, as the committee so decides. It is impossible to discuss the report as a whole, because the committee may agree with some of the changes and oppose others.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
How long are we going to take to dispose of the recommendations contained in what has been called the beginning of the report? We are starting in the middle. Are we going to go back to that, or ignore it?
Mr. MACKENZIE (Vancouver Centre)-: I should be inclined to ignore it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
One who proposes anything in connection with the rules has to take some responsibility. The hon. member has asked a pertinent question, namely, when do we proceed from the general to the particular, and when do we know that we have finished with the general discussion? If, Mr. Speaker, who is carrying this particular item on the order paper, would consent, and if the committee would consent, even though it may be irregular, that the first item might be called as it has been called now, with no, limitations imposed except those which are imposed by the subjects discussed in the so-called preamble or the general introduction to the report; on that item full discussion might then take place on any of the subjects which are in the minds of hon. members. When that item is disposed of, the general discussion would be concluded, and we would then proceed with the different amendments which are to be dealt with. 1

Rules of the House

can understand that the general discussion in some respects will not be germane to the particular amendment to standing order 9, which is the first item. But at the same time if we all agree that it would mark the termination of the general discussion when the amendment is actually passed or disposed of, then the other items could be proceeded with. If we adopt that procedure we may get along.
I am sure that in amending the rules of the house we do not want to transgress the present rules more than is necessary and make the discussion any less regular than it would be under the rules we are endeavouring to amend. I cannot see how we are ever going to do anything practical if we just have a general discussion without terminating it with some sort of action by the committee on the items itself respecting standing order 9. It seems to me that the method proposed might provide a termination point for the general discussion.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, for the last few seconds the discussion has been over spilt milk. You have rendered a very wise decision. You have decided according to the wish of the committee. This is the very best kind of decision that anyone in the chair can render.
There are things that I disapprove and others that I approve. One of the things that I approve very highly is the fact that the Prime Minister notified the house a week ago that to-day, Tuesday, April 25, we would take up this matter. As a rule at eleven o'clock at night the government does not know what will come before the house the day following, but in this case we were told a week ahead. That is a good practice, which should be followed with respect to the agenda for every day of the session. Members should be notified long in advance of what is to come up on certain days, so that they can prepare themselves for discussion.
I have said that the first part of the committee's report is a preamble. His Honour the Speaker said that it was the basis for all the amendments proposed to the rules. That shows the importance of the matter, and I wonder if that preamble should not be read in' the same fashion as a prologue to a Shakespearian tragedy. And what would be the tragedy? The tragedy would be that each member of parliament would put his head on the block, to deprive himself of rights that our forefathers gained for us.
What was the purpose of the amendments to the rules in 1927? It was to allow the Prime Minister, the leader of the opposition and some of the cabinet ministers to use some of the time of the private members; it gave them full latitude at the expense of the

rights of private members, whose speeches were curtailed to forty minutes. The rights of members of parliament were taken away by those amendments, and the same sort of thing is proposed to-day. Why is it done? It is because of the fear that the government and the opposition have of the yellow press, which has been complaining, not of the government, not of the opposition, but of the role of parliament. I defy the press tycoons of Montreal, Winnipeg or anywhere else to discuss that matter with a member of parliament who knows what the rights of a member of parliament are. What are the rights of a member of parliament? It is shameful that in this country those who do not know anything about the work performed by members of parliament dare to criticize us and vilify us before the people. Long enough have members of parliament been considered nonentities. Long enough have members of parliament not been consulted on matters of great national concern, but have been told instead that such and such a matter is a military secret or that it was none of their business to be informed of the progress of the administration, whether in the right way or in the wrong way. But this is an abdication of the rights of parliament to be signed by ourselves. Are members of parliament going to sign the decree of execution of their own rights, the rights for which our forefathers fought so hard more than a century ago?
And now because some tycoon who is receiving a big rent for the selective service administration building here in Ottawa, and another one who is after all the ministers who have contracts for fine paper in Montreal, and another one who is here all the time seeking jobs, are so much concerned about the vigilance of members of parliament in denouncing them when they get things like that at the expense of the taxpayer, we are to have amendments to the rules of the house. I denounce these tycoons most bitterly as the enemies and foes of the common people. We must be respected, and we must be respected by the government as members of parliament if we want to be respected by our own constituents. We deserve more respect precisely from those who desire to curtail the rights of members of parliament to denounce them when they do wrong. That is why I feel so much humiliated on reading the preface which is the basis of the amendments, these uncalled for and untimely amendments that are proposed.
Why should members of parliament willingly abandon their own rights? Some members who sat on that committee had a smile on their lips. It would save the time of the

Rules of the House
House of Commons, they said. Would it not save time if we had proper accounts? Would it not save time if the public accounts were just as good to-day as they were when Mr. Robb was Minister of Finance and Mr. Gonthier, a French Canadian, was auditor general?
But now it is different. Even the leader of the opposition, who is a genial fellow, rises in his place and says, "I do not want to take up too much of the time of the house." He has the right to take up as much time of the house as he wishes. Why should he apologize when he rises to speak, if he has something important to say? There is no reason for his apologizing at all, or for any member of parliament excusing himself for rising in this House of Commons to voice the complaints of his constituents. I do not see why there should be such an inferiority complex in members of parliament towards the government or towards the leader of the opposition or of any group.
Once someone wrote to the chairman asking him if there was not a precedent for some people speaking in committee. There are no precedents, Mr. Chairman, and if there were one, it would be the precedent of service to the country by a member of parliament. Long service? I never claimed it. I believe we are all equals. But I believe that my colleagues and myself deserve the respect of the Canadian people, and it is shameful, sir, that some press tycoons, taking advantage of the fact that they do not sign their articles, throw insults in the faces of members of parliament.
Sir, we must have some dignity. We have some rights. Let us keep them. I strongly protest against the three first pages of this so-called prologue or preamble. It is shameful. There is no reason to have those three pages in the record of parliament. It must be voted down; and then I shall be ready to discuss the amendments without fear or favour.
In my view all members of parliament should be on the same footing. There is no reason why anyone, whether the Prime Minister or the Leader of the Opposition, should be entitled to any more time than the least back-bencher on either side of the house. All members of parliament, whether on the treasury benches or to the rear of them, should have the same rights. I do not see why members have to curtail their speeches to forty minutes, except it be to give more time to others who are regarded as more important than private members in this chamber. But why should that be? It is opposed to the first principles of democracy.
We contend that Canada should be on an equal footing with other nations; let us in the first place be equals amongst ourselves. That is the first thing. Then, let us have enough esprit de corps to join together to censure those journalists who spend their time in throwing contempt on members of parliament. Personally I am indifferent to their attacks; I have proved that again and again. They do not impress me. When anyone does his duty, why should he be fearful of criticism?
I ask my fellow members kindly to consider these matters, to read the first three pages of the paper which is before them; and then I invite them to reflect upon what they will say to their constituents when the general elections come, when someone may read tc them the first sentence of this report:
Your committee, in the performance of the important duty assigned to it by the house, has taken into account the existence of general criticism of parliament both by members and representative citizens.
Who are the members of parliament who have criticized parliament itself? Where are they? If there are any, let them raise their hands. I do not see anyone raise his hand. The chamber is full of members, but not one has raised his hand, and there is no one who will dare to do that. Then, who are these representative citizens? One daily newspaper in Ottawa, one in Montreal, one in Winnipeg, have spoken against the fact that members of parliament are voicing the complaints of their constituents here in this chamber. That is what we are here for.
I have said enough to bring to the attention of hon. members this most important matter, which has been overlooked by all those who were on that committee. It is not by kneeling down before the press that parliament will be respected. We can defend ourselves; our parliamentary life is an open book, and they have only to look at the records of parliament to see that we are not responsible for the legislation which is passed by a stroke of the pen by some individuals, contrary to the old way of passing legislation. But nevertheless we are doing our best to help our constituents -in a different way, if you wish. I admit that my hon. friends opposite are animated by as much good-will as those on this side of the chamber. I have never questioned their good-will, nor have I ever imputed motives to them, not merely because I desire to act in accordance with the rules of the house, but also to show my good-will towards them. I have been associated with members of parliament for twenty years, and I do not complain about that association. I think that members of parliament are a lot of good
Rules of the House

fellows, working together in difficult circumstances, trying to do the best they can for their people, and they deserve something better than this. If someone says "This is an innocuous remark, you must pass it over and pay no attention to it"-as the Minister of Pensions and National Health has just said-that is childish. We must consider what will happen to our official status if this is passed; we must weigh it on its own merit. My fear is that it will be a stigma which will be attachsd to members of parliament, especially to the one who has just spoken, and who will be defeated at the next election by a tremendous majority-and for the good of the country-and that hon. members will sink down under public opprobrium.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: The leader of the house made the suggestion that in order to obtain some finality with regard to our discussion to-day the first amendment should be considered as an open amendment with a general discussion to take place upon it; and after that discussion has been had, and the first amendment passed or rejected, that we go on to the other amendments. He put the question to me whether I would be agreeable to that. I of course am perfectly agreeable to it. Perhaps it can be understood that on the first amendment there shall be the general discussion which would have taken place in the ordinary course prior to it, and when that is completed and the first amendment passed, we can then proceed to the other amendments on their terms.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
May I ask the Speaker a question? While that seems a very suitable solution, there is this objection to it. When you are dealing with the amendment to standing order 9, it is to be agreed that we are to discuss the general subject, and when that passes we go on to the next amendment. But that will not afford us an opportunity to vote on these two other recommendations which the report contains and which do not happen to be amendments of standing orders. That is where the mistake has arisen. Certain recommendations have been made. Some of them are quite good and worthy of consideration, and we ought to vote on them. We want an oportunity to vote on each one of them. If that could be arranged, I think the thing would go along quite smoothly.
As regards what has been termed the preamble, the Minister of Pensions and National Health suggested that we should "forget it". Well, that is not a very polite way of dealing with a recommendation of the committee. I believe that the Prime Minister said the other day that we should regard the first portion of the report with something like mental

reserve-not pay too much attention to it, he said. But that is not my view. There is a definite recommendation in the earlier part of the report on page 2. I want an opportuntiy to discuss it and to vote on it. That seems reasonable enough.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: What part is that?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
In what is called the preamble. I read it out a moment ago. They make two definite recommendations:
We therefore recommend that, when the yearly estimates have been brought down, one day a week be set aside for consideration of supply. If that is done, the house is not likely to find itself under the necessity of passing a great part of the estimates in the dying days of the session.
I think that is a good idea; I would vote for it. But that is not the point. The next recommendation is:
Our recommendation is that, when there is reason to believe that debate will be protracted, parties and groups recognized in the house shall confer-[DOT]
It does not say, with whom.
-and make arrangements either for allotting days or laying any plan for saving time. . . .
And so on.
I strongly object to that-there is the more need for discussion. But let us do something about it; it is a definite recommendation. It is suggested now that we should start in the middle of the report and go on from there, and the minister of pensions says, "Let us forget the first part". I think it would be a good idea to forget the whole thing.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I cannot follow the reasoning of the hon. member with regard to the first part of the report. It is not intended that anything in the first part of the report shall be an alteration in the procedure of the house. What is intended by the report dealing especially with the standing orders of the house is what is contained in the latter part of the report, and to that the attention of the committee is recommended. The first portion of the report, to which my hon. friend has referred, is purely the thought of the committee; it is theoretical, it has no bearing, and cannot be amended by anything the committee could do because it does not change the standing orders of the house. All that will be changed, if the report is adopted, are the amendments that are proposed, to be found on page 4.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: How can we accept or reject these recommendations without dealing with them?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
The hon. member may make his protest with regard to it, and when the time comes, if it ever does, that an amend-

Rules oj the House
ment is made to the standing order, the hon. gentleman will have the right to propose an amendment. At the moment, however, an amendment cannot be moved to the first portion of the report which would have an effect on our standing orders. All that we have to-day before us are the amendments, and these only can alter the standing orders. I suggest to the committee that on the first amendment with which we are dealing the general discussion should take place, and that immediately it is disposed of we proceed to the other amendments.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: On the point raised by the hon. member for Weyburn, which was properly answered by the leader of the house, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), it was the intention of the chair first of all to call the proposed amendments one by one, and that is why the first was called, so as to allow a general discussion.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: That is not the first one.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
The first proposed
amendment. There are ten which are enumerated in the document I have before me. In the matter brought up by the leader of the house, as to when the discussion will terminate, we have in this instance a procedure similar to that in connection with the war appropriation bill, and I believe hon. members as well as the minister himself realized that we secured a great deal of cooperation so far as the general discussion was concerned. When we feel that the time has arrived when we can properly proceed with the proposed amendments, the general discussion will be terminated. We will follow the same procedure in this instance as in the war appropriation bill.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I think His Honour the
Speaker has clarified in the minds of most hon. members of the committee what it is that we are about to do. It is distinctly understood that the committee is not going to pass, nor will it become the law of the house, what has been termed the preamble. That understanding will obviate a great deal of discussion. I take it from the remarks of the Speaker that we are about either to pass or to reject the recommendations which are numbered, and if passed they will become the rule of the house. But the opening observations of the committee simply stand as their considered opinion and are in no way binding on the members of the committee.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
With all due deference to what has been said by the member for New Westminster, my understanding of parliamentary procedure is that when a committee makes a special and final report and
uses such language as "we therefore recommend", which has been referred to by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, that recommendation is followed by something that is relevant to it. But can anyone show me where in the recommendations that follow there is any reference to one day a week being set aside for consideration of supply? Yet the committee in their preamble, or whatever you choose to call it, deliberately use these words, "we therefore recommend". I would ask any member of the committee, I would ask you, Mr. Chairman, to show me where there is a reference to that language in the recommendations themselves. I suggest that it is superfluous and we ought to clear up that point. I accept, as the member for Comox-Alberni does, this language inserted by a special committee of this house as being definitely a recommendation to the house, and I do not see how it can be discarded as being merely idle and useless words.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I move, Mr. Chairman,
that pages 1, 2 and 3 of the introduction be struck out of the report.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
It has been moved
that paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 of the introduction be struck out of the report.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Pages, not paragraphs.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Pages, Mr. Chairman. To support my amendment-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I shall have to rule
the amendment out of order for the reason that the introduction is not before the committee. We have the word of His Honour the Speaker, as everyone will readily see, that we are dealing only with the proposed amendments to the rules of procedure of the House of Commons, so that the introduction is not before the committee.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
If you will permit me,
sir, I submit that what we have before us is not the interpretation of His Honour the Speaker but certain sheets of paper that are here and that we see with our eyes. It is not enough to say that. certain language is not before us. That was not the meaning of my motion at all. What I expected was that the committee would show its disapproval of what is contained in these three pages. It is not a matter of our passing them over. The point is that as members of parliament we cannot accept what has been said in that introduction without becoming the laughingstock of the country, and that is why I have moved to strike out those pages. At present it is not a question of His Honour giving his interpretation. His Honour is not in the chair; it is the chairman who is in the chair.
Rules of the House

I submit that these pages form part of the official .document. I regret that the signature of the chairman of the committee is not on this report, as it should have been if it were a true copy. We always see the signature of the chairman on reports that come from committees. This is a special committee but there is no signature. That, however, is a small point on which I will not insist. I hope that the committee will consider the seriousness of the situation and will not kneel down before those who try to depreciate our parliamentary institutions-those outside the house who do that job. I will therefore ask you, sir, to be good enough to reconsider your ruling. I will not appeal from it, because I do not like that kind of procedure, and I resort to it as little as possible. I hope however you will reconsider that ruling in the light of what has been said, which is an insult as much to you as to any other hon. member of the house, including Mr. Speaker. I protest strongly against it.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Is there a motion before the committee? If there is not a motion I do not see how we can vote on it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: The hon. member was not in the chamber when I called the first proposed amendment to the attention of the sommittee.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: But there is no motion before the house. *

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Yes. There is a motion.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: His Honour the Speaker was chairman of this committee. I want to get myself clear on this before we proceed.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: You had better.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I will refrain from saying what was passing through my mind. I will ask His Honour to clarify this point. Probably I am not as brilliant as my hon. friend across the floor who interrupted. When language like this is used, "we therefore recommend that one day be set aside for supply," why is it that there is no properly written amendment in what follows later on to carry out that recommendation? To me these words are definite. That was in the mind of the committee, and I should like to know why there is no such amendment. I should like to know the reason for that, because these words, "we recommend" appear to me to be one of the most important things * dealt with in the whole report.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
If the hon. member will look at page 2 of the report he will see these words:
The procedure required to keep this privilege unimpaired


That is with regard to the estimates being referred to a standing committee. Then it goes on:
Certain estimates may be occasionally referred to a select committee in order to ascertain facts which the house desires to know, but this practice should be adopted guardedly and -only in very special circumstances. Your committee does not think it would be advisable to change the present system and it believes that the elasticity of the present rules makes it possible to apply them in new situations from time to time. We, however, desire to submit that considerable time could be saved if the committee of supply sat oftener in the early part of the session. We therefore recommend that, when the yearly estimates have been brought down, one day a -week be set aside for consideration of supply.
The next sentence is:
If this is done the house is not likely to find itself under the necessity of passing a great part of the estimates in the dying days of the session.
It was the thought of the committee that some procedure should be adopted with regard to the estimates, but they were not in a position to suggest an amendment and in fact rather deprecated the idea of making suggestions at this time in regard to the manner of dealing with the estimates.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Then that was definitely in the mind of the committee, if they wished to insert that reference into their report.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: They were definitely dealing with that matter; yes.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Then could you explain why there is no reference to it in the recommendations?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I think they were almost unanimously of the opinion that this was not a proper time to make any change with regard to the submission of the estimates to the house, and at the beginning of that paragraph the reasons for that decision are set out. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the amendment which has been moved is not in order. There are no recommendations before the committee in this preamble; there are no amendments set out in pages 1, 2 and 3. At the moment we are dealing only with standing order 9, so that I think the amendment is out of order.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
If I may say another word, the statement has been made that there is no motion before the committee. I submit that there is a motion before the committee, the motion for further consideration in committee of the whole of the report of the special committee on the revision of standing orders and this is what we are considering to-day. We are considering the revision of the rules; we are

Rules oj the House
revising the standing orders. We are not passing the first three pages; we are dealing with the rules of the house, and that is what is before this committee.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
May I remind you, Mr. Chairman, that the special committee sent us a report which contained an introduction. The report was discussed in this committee on a previous occasion, and progress was reported; to-day we are resuming that discussion. The report of the special committee cannot possibly be changed unless it is amended by this committee. No one has the power to delete the introduction to the report that was presented to this house. It was not the report of one or two gentlemen; it was the report of a special committee to the committee of the whole, in which we are now sitting. Now the special committee has vanished, after its final report has been presented, and the committee of the whole is the only body that can change the report. I positively deny what has been said by any minister or any other hon. gentleman to the effect that the first part of the report is not before this committee. It is, by the very fact that no one but this committee has a right to change the report.
My second contention, Mr. Chairman, is that we cannot deal with this report unless it is put in better shape by a revived special committee. Was it not the Prime Minister himself who suggested that the paragraphs should be numbered and who expressed dissatisfaction with the introduction? I agree that the introduction should go; but even if it is not on the pieces of paper which have been placed before you, Mr. Chairman, it is before the committee just the same, because it is part of the report of the special committee to this committee. That being so, I would ask you to reconsider your ruling and to decide that the introduction should be deleted from the report of the special committee, just as it has been deleted from the pieces of paper that are before you. After that is done we will have a breathing spell in which to consider the amendments.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I should like to give my heartiest [DOT]support to the suggestion of the hon. member for Temiscouata; I am in perfect accord with what has been said by him and by the hon. member for Comox-Albemi. There must be a reason for everything. If this preamble is not worth looking at, I do not know why it is here. Furthermore, as was pointed out by a previous speaker to my right, this preamble is full of recommendations which are very important, but which are not followed up by suggested amendments in the remainder of the report. If this introduction is not to be
studied before we deal with the amendments there is no need to have it there at all. Moreover, it is dangerous to retain it. Just to give an example of the danger involved in this preamble I should like to quote a few lines from it. At the bottom of page 2 I read this:
Our recommendation is that when there is reason to believe that debate will be protracted, parties and groups recognized in the house shall confer and make ararngements either for allotting days or laying any plan for saving time whilst protecting freedom of speech for every representative of the people who sits in this house.
That is a very important recommendation, and many others are contained in this introduction. If we should take up the amendments and adopt the whole report, the introduction together with its recommendations would have to be adopted as well. That is the danger I want to bring to the attention of the committee. Moreover, not only recommendations of this kind are contained in the preamble; we find also some contradictions of great importance. Hon. members have just heard what I have read from page 2. I say that suggestion is not in accordance with the premise appearing on the first page. It sets forth a principle which is not in accordance with what I have just read.
In the third paragraph of the first page, at line 13 we find this:
Parliament is the assembly of representatives elected by the people where great issues are debated, or should be debated; it is not primarily a body of auditors charged with the inspection of departmental accounts. Freedom of speech is one of the inalienable privileges of members of the House of Commons. It is in truth the privilege of their constituents and it is secured to members not for their personal benefit but to enable them to discharge the funtions of their office. Without it, the essence of the country's liberty does not exist.
Apparently that principle is not taken into account when it is suggested that when debates are protracted there should be some kind of agreement among the recognized groups or parties, and that private members must not have anything to do with any decision so made. Why include the recognized groups? Why not the opposition and the government only, or the government alone? That would look even more like Hitler's way of governing a country.
As I said before, we should study the introduction, and see what we are going to do with it. The amendment proposed to standing order 49 is as follows:
Only one amendment and one subamendment may be made to the motion for the address in reply to the speech from the throne and to the motion for the Speaker to leave the chair for the house to go into committee of supply or ways and means.
Rules of the House

Here is an amendment which restricts the very principle set forth in the first page of the introduction. How can we accept this amendment? How can we accept that suggestion with respect to the understanding which should be arrived at among groups or parties, if at the same time we are to recognize this other principle? There is too much contradiction in that. That is why I support the suggestion made by the hon. member for Temiscouata to the effect that either we discuss the introduction fully, before we study the amendments themselves, or that it should be stricken from the report.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I hardly know where we stand. I understand the hon. member for Temiscouata moved an amendment to delete the introduction, and that you have ruled it out of order. Nevertheless the hon. member who has just taken his seat made a lengthy speech in support of that amendment. Surely we should have matters clear in our minds. I see no reason for such confusion. Mr. Speaker made the situation quite clear. The only observation I would make, possibly to make it somewhat clearer, is that the word "recommend", in the two instances where they occur in the introduction, should be changed to "suggest". I say that because the committee is not, in fact, recommending. There are general matters within the ambit of the government's right in organizing the business of the house. The committee was merely making a suggestion that the government should follow a certain procedure. With this further clarification of what Mr. Speaker has already said I would hope that we might now proceed with the discussion of the specific amendment to the standing order proposed by the committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: The hon. member for Vancouver East has made the suggestion with regard to the word "recommend". I entirely agree that the meaning of the whole paragraph would be more clear in the minds of all hon. members if the word had been "suggest" instead of "recommend". That, I may say, was the intention of the committee. It was not the intention to recommend; rather it was to suggest. The very words in the paragraph indicate that we were making no recommendation; rather it was to be a matter for consideration by the government of the day. The hon. member for Vancouver East is perfectly right when he says that the word "suggest" would convey the meaning of the committee better than the word which was used.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Unfortunately we are dealing with what was said, not what was thought.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
May I add a word to what I said earlier in the afternoon? First of all may I compliment Mr. Speaker, Mr. Deputy Speaker and the Clerk of the House. These three gentlemen especially have been performing great public services in a time of war.
There is no doubt that in war time, rules are to a great extent unwritten. That has been so in the British parliament. In some instances before us now changes have been very radical, while in others they have been of minor importance. One of the points which I thought might have been considered was considered in England ten years ago. I have in mind parliamentary reform, constitutional reform, cabinet and law reform, and a more equitable division of the work of parliament between the two houses, namely the House of Commons and the one in another place.
In my view more latitude should be allowed for the asking of supplementary questions, more than the three mentioned in the report, especially in a time of war. For instance, it was not until the 119th day of the last session that the matter of foreign affairs was discussed in this house. An amendment has been suggested with respect to questions asked when the orders of the day are called. When the committee reported there was a statement to the effect that no hon. member had written making any request. The fact is that both one year ago' and two years ago I wrote letters of that kind, and gave copies to leaders in the house. It was not necessary, I said, to pass a resolution in order to allow us to put supplementary questions to ministers when the orders of the day are called.
In England standing order 9 provides that questions which have not appeared on the order paper, but which are of an urgent nature and relate either to matters of great public importance or to a rearrangement of the business of the house, may be put at the opening of a sitting, extending from a quarter to three to a quarter to four. Under that rule members have an opportunity practically to cross-examine the ministry in respect of matters of great public importance.
I have in mind a new book issued in 1930 by G. F. M. Campion, then second clerk, now Clerk of the House of Commons at Westminster, who has since been knighted.
I believe the book written by our own learned and able Clerk compares most favourably with this great text book, which, in part, states:
Not later than three o'clock the question hour begins. This is a more important item of

Rules of the House
business than any yet described. It is expected to provide lively moments and seems to be of unfailing interest to members and the public. It is modern and affords a useful method of supervising the administration of the government. Its effectiveness is generally recognized. Questions 'turn a searchlight upon every corner of the public service.' (Lowell, i. 332). Their chief object is 'the explanation to the public of the meaning of political events/ and They are often arranged by the government itself, so as to give them an opportunity of making announcements in a somewhat informal way.' (Redlich, ii. 241 and 242). They are 'serviceable as obviating the necessity in many instances of more extended debate and of motions for papers. (Todd, 1982, ii. 85). And finally, 'questions afford to the private member under modern conditions almost his only opportunity.' (Marriott, i. 571).
Under standing order 1 of our rules, according to the Parliamentary Rules and Forms, so well written and edited by our learned Clerk, in all eases not provided for in our orders, the usages and customs of the British house as in force at the time shall be followed. Under our rules as they are at present an hon. member should have the latitude on the orders of the day of asking these supplementary questions, because it is a useful method of supervising the administration of the government. Its effectiveness is generally recognized. Questions turn a searchlight upon every comer of the public service. Their chief object is the explanation to the public of the meaning of political events, and in the old country they are often arranged by the government itself so as to give them an opportunity of making announcements in a somewhat informal way. I think the rule recommended by this report before us allows only three supplementary questions. In view of the importance of the war I think that more questions than three should be permitted, because it would mean saving time.
There are only one or two other matters that I should like to refer to. I should like to say a word about select committees and special committees of the house with reference to the submitting of expenditures of money to these committees. Very little value has been obtained in that way. The same thing applies to the finding of facts and obtaining of information through committee work. Take the railways and shipping committee. It was a special committee. It has now been made a standing committee. They meet and hold three or four meetings and then adjourn. A report is brought in. At the last session it was brought in the last day but one of the session. There is very little control over those expenditures. Steps were taken in England three hundred years ago to give parliament control over the executive and a civil war was fought there to secure such control. To-day we are back where we were
two hundred years ago. There is a war on and four billion dollars have been expended. What do we know about it? We have the war expenditures committee sitting but we cannot discuss the report. So far as the members of the house are concerned they are forgotten now as a body by their special committees and references to control boards and commissions. Practically all our rights, privileges and functions have been taken away, with the result that the high court of parliament has been turned into something which it was never intended to be. We are a legislative body and those other bodies are created with executive powers. In the olden days under the constitution the executive was the cabinet, but to-day we have such a number of these control bodies and their subcontrols-there are now nearly one hundred -that parliament has divested itself in actual practice of any control over one dollar of expenditures.
What I point out to the committee is this:
I believe the time has come to adopt constitutional reform. I proposed it fifteen or twenty years ago when I first came into the house. I proposed that we adopt the municipal system of supervising the estimates of the public departments. I suggested that the committee of the whole house be given the power to suggest to the minister that for economy purposes he reduce his estimates ten per cent, twenty per cent, thirty per cent or whatever the committee saw fit to do. That is what is done under the municipal organizations where the expenditures of the heads of departments are supervised. Under our constitution, which has been in existence for two hundred years, that cannot be done because if one dollar is struck off the estimates the cabinet must resign and a new election be called. I suggest that something along these lines should be done. I believe that the time has come to assign to the other branch of parliament in another place some executive powers and further powers in war time. They made that reform in England in the House of Lords at least fifteen years ago with the result that when the war came along they were found to be doing good work. The Prime Minister suggested a select committee be appointed to look into the Ottawa agreement. He sug-' gested that that should be a joint committee of the two houses. We have had this committee on the revision of the rules sitting during the war, and some of the recommendations that they have made are very good. But further power by changes of rules should be assigned to the other branch of parliament.
The other matter I should like to refer to has to do with public bills versus private bills.
Rules of the House

There is a whole list of these private bills on the order paper. They come mainly from the other place, since they are largely divorce bills. At the end of the session they are put through. Bills of business concerns originate in the other place and that should as private bills originate here. There should be some check and control over that. Public bills of private members have been relegated to the last page on the order paper. They may as well not be moved. While some of the agencies of these public bills would assist the conduct of public business, parliament has ignored them since the war started and for many years before, and this parliament has been losing its prestige in the country. The taxpayers of the country are the people who pay the bills. The members of the House of Commons do their part, but the large body outside the house, the man in the street and on the bus pays the bills. This is the only forum that I know of where the average man on the street can get his grievances remedied. When this parliament ceases to function as such, parliamentary government is at an end. The private member is the connecting link between the government of the day and the elector, and when he ceases to function efficient parliamentary government is at an end. The rights and privileges of the private member have been curtailed and thus taken away from him. He cannot ask a single emergency question in war time without coming in conflict at times with the rules. We have been very fortunate in our Speaker and Deputy Speaker in that they have sensed the feeling of the house, as has our learned Clerk. But I say, Mr. Chairman, that there could be more latitude given to the consideration of public bills in order to improve the conditions of the taxpayers who pay the bills. They should have precedence over the private bill of some individual or some company that seeks legislation mainly for its own benefit.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
On page 2
of the report which is now before us, I notice the following:
Your committee, in all its deliberations, has kept in mind the importance of not impairing the rights of minorities.
I believe that we have started the discussion of this report the wrong way in interfering on two different occasions with the rights of minorities. In the first place, I asked one of the pages to bring me a French copy of the report, but the French translation is not yet ready. I do protest, Mr. Chairman-and those who know me are aware that I harbour no feelings of bitter fanaticism-I do protest against the fact that such an important report has not been printed both in French and in

English and distributed to French-speaking members in their own language.
I take this opportunity to protest against the practice which is followed in this house of distributing official documents in one language only.
I should, of course, have liked to have more time at my disposal in order to make a detailed analysis of this report, which amends to a considerable extent the rules of parliamentary procedure.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: For the information of the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Lalonde), I may say that the committee's report was published in the French language in the French edition of the Votes and Proceedings of the House of Commons on Friday, March 3, 1944, as well as in the official report of debates on Tuesday, March 7.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I thank the chairman of
the committee for that information, which I had already obtained, but I do protest against the fact that French copies of the report have not been made available to French-speaking hon. members. The other minority groups to which I refer are able to take care of themselves and I shall not take up their defence. The hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy) has emphasized his opposition to rule 49. On page 9 I notice the following:
The debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne covers the whole ground of administration and is repeated when the budget is brought down. This debate has been abolished in the House of Assembly of South Africa where the following standing order is now in force: "Mr. Speaker shall report to this House the Governor General's speech, and there shall be no debate on such report."
Your committee felt that the house could not abolish this debate, but it realized that the scope of discussion was so wide and the question of relevancy almost non-existent on this particular occasion that the freedom of speech of every member, party or group -would be fully preserved by limiting the number of amendments in the same way as on the motion for committee of supply. These two motions are in the same category, namely, they furnish occasions for airing grievances and making suggestions to the government.
And the amendment which ia suggested, Mr. Chairman, is as follows:
Only one amendment and one subamendment may be made to the motion for the address in reply to the speech from the throne and to the motion for the speaker to leave the chair for the house to go into committee of supply or ways and means.
Must I understand, Mr. Chairman, that only one amendment will be permitted, or, on the other hand, will any member of the house be permitted, if his amendment is relevant to the main motion, to move as many subamend-

Rules oj the House
merits as he likes provided they are discussed one after the other? Otherwise, if just one subamendment is permitted I cannot see how the rights of the minorities in this chamber will be protected. I understand that any member of the house has the right to move a subamendment to an amendment provided he is within the scope of the main motion or the amendment.
I would like to have a clear explanation from the Chair or from Mr. Speaker concerning this proposed amendment to our standing orders.
Without prejudice to what I have said, Mr. Chairman, I shall now conclude those brief remarks, in expressing the hope that they be favourably considered by yourself and the members of the committee.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I would like to have an answer to my question if possible, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: As the hon. member for Labelle realizes, we called the first proposed amendment and allowed a general discussion. The question he has asked is pertinent to another proposed amendment which we shall reach later, and then his last question could be more readily answered.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I thank you very much, Mr. Chairman. I will be there to discuss it when we reach it.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: If the amendment to standing order 9 passes, it automatically passes the whole of the preamble, which contains two definite recommendations which I wish to discuss. This committee did not agree to that. The chairman has just told the hon. member that that was the arrangement. That was not the arrangement, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, there is no question with which the government officially has as little to do as on a question of this kind. It is a question absolutely for members of the house, and I would not intervene in any way except perhaps to th6 extent that I may have some responsibility for assisting in promoting regularity of debate and helping to expedite, if I may, the business of the house. The hon. member for Comox-Albemi is perfectly right. There was no agreement that the suggestion I made would be accepted. But is not the situation this? There is at this minute before the house an amendment to standing order 9 which has been regularly moved and which has been called by the Chair and which is now open for debate. Some objection was taken to
discussing standing order 9 before discussion of what was called the prologue or preliminary part of the report, and it was suggested then, in order that there might be the greatest latitude possible, that we should have some general discussion of the preliminary part and of some of the principles which were there laid down. Then I had the temerity to suggest that in order to regularize debate and to know when the general discussion- had ceased and when we were embarked on the job of dealing with the different amendments in order-in other words, to provide some terminal facilities for the general discussion'-we treat the general discussion as taking place on the amendment to standing order 9, and that when the amendment to standing order 9 was disposed of, either voted down or agreed to or amended, the general discussion would be over and we would go on with the other amendments.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: That is just my objection. The general discussion would then be over, and the preliminary part of the report which comes under the general discussion contains two recommendations on which I wish to speak. If the amendment to standing order 9 passes, that other part goes through automatically. I protest against that, and I think I am within my rights when I say I want an opportunity to vote on the two recommendations contained in the earlier part of the report.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
My suggestion does not meet my hon. friend's desires if he wants an opportunity to vote as well as to discuss the two recommendations he mentions, but it does provide him with ample opportunity to discuss them, because I suggested that the general discussion, including the two recommendations my hon. friend mentions, take place on the item now before the Chair. I thought that was probably sufficient for members of the house. I have looked at these two recommendations and I think my hon. friend will agree with me that no changes in the standing orders are required to give effect to them. One is a recommendation with regard to regulation of the business of the house, and the other is more or less of a pious recommendation, if I may say so with all respect to the committee, that people of good will shall confer one witii the other with regard to the conduct of the business of the house. That is not something which you could embody in a standing order or in a regulation. So it seemed to me that all that was necessary in connection with either of these recommendations mentioned by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni was that they be discussed and perhaps their futility, if that is the opinion of some members of the
Rules of the House

house, be exposed or their merits proclaimed, if that is the opinion of some other members; and then call it a day so far as those preliminary recommendations or suggestions are concerned.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: But we cannot vote on them.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
If my hon. friend wants an opportunity to take the opinion of the house upon them, the only way I can suggest, and I do not know whether it is in order or not, is that after we have disposed of the items somebody might bring in a motion either censuring the committee or commending the committee and provide an opportunity to vote on his motion. I mean that seriously; I am not sarcastic. It seems to me that that would be one way of dealing with it. I cannot imagine that it would be quite in order for a committee of the house solemnly to express the opinion that the government might do so and so in the way of arranging business of the house or that groups should confer about procedure. I would regard that merely as a suggestion which could be acted upon or otherwise as they thought fit.
May I suggest that perhaps some members have read this preamble or prologue too critically. All it does is to indicate that there have been criticisms of procedure in the house but that those criticisms are more or less based on a misconception, and it endeavours to point out those misconceptions. In any case, I suggest to my hon. friend that those criticisms really have not much to do with the recommendations to which he refers. If he himself feels that he should criticize the committee for making those remarks, well and good, but that does not get him very far in wanting to vote on those two particular recommendations.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I want to vote for one and against the other. How am I to do that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
If the hon. member asks my advice, I would simply make the statement he has now made and give his reasons for it, and he has plenty of opportunity to do that in the debate. He can be sure of this, that in connection with the one he wants to vote against, the fact that there is no vote now will not prevent him from voting against it if it should ever come up, because this committee will not have passed on it favourably, will not have approved it. Therefore at any time that anyone wants to adopt the proposal which he says he is against, it will be open to him, he can be sure, to oppose it. With regard to the recommendation of which he is in favour, it is true that he does not get the opportunity of finding out whether the committee is with him on that particular point, but I would say here again that the

fact that he has not just now an opportunity to support it will not prevent him from voting for it whenever it should come up in some regular form. I assume that the one of which he is in favour is that with regard to supply.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I do not know that I have to state my case, but that happens to be it. All I ask is the opportunity to vote on a definite recommendation made by a committee of this house. The minister can explain it away as he likes, but I am not going to be deprived of my rights, and there are others here who share my views.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
