speechtext: L am sure my hon. friend has misunderstood me entirely. I thought he was trying to explain what recommendations he favoured and what recommendations he was against. I withdraw my question entirely. I do not want him to disclose anything he does not want to disclose. The only reason I wanted to know which he was in favour of was to find out if he was in any way prejudiced because he was not able at this time to vote, because the committee would not be dealing with his particular question.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: The minister is correct.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I do not know what the question is. However, I submit to the committee, as a humble member of the house, like anyone else, that we have some pretty important amendments before us, which do afford opportunity for a full discussion of important questions of procedure, questions which involve not only the saving of time but the expediting of business generally. I suggest that, if that be the fact, there is a definite recommendation before the committee. There is full opportunity of discussing the report. Nobody has seen fit to bring forward the two recommendations to which Pay hon. friend refers, and neither of them I have pointed out, is germane to an amendment of the standing orders. I submit that we should proceed now as members of the house to the discussion of the first amendment, including a full discussion if it is desired, by everyone who is interested, on the two recommendations to which my hon. friend refers, although they are not embodied in the amendment of the standing orders. Then when we have discussed that, we can deal with the other amendments to the standing orders and go through with them. I tell my hon. friend that I will do the best I can to see if I can find any procedure under which he can get this committee or some committee of the house on record with regard to the two recommendations in which he is interested. I believe that when he comes to think the thing over he will content himself, as other hon. members have contented them-

Rules oj the House
selves, with expressing an opinion on a recommendation which is purely a suggestion and which is not before this committee, and leaving that opinion on record to be implemented by his vote whenever that recommendation comes up for actual discussion and decision by the house.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Pardon me; it is before the house.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I do not think it is. It is not before the committee. The motion before the committee is the amendment of standing order 9.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: We have never reached that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: It has been called. My hon. friend will remember that there was a distinct agreement, I think on everybody's part, that the job to be done was to put these recommendations in order and number-that is, the recommendations which were recommendations with regard to standing orders.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: It has not been done. They are not numbered.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: They are in order. It was agreed to put them in order so that they might be dealt with as resolutions.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Except the two.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: But the two are not amendments of standing orders.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: No, I did not say they were.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: And they are not amendments of the procedure set out in this book of parliamentary rules.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I never said they were, but they are recommendations of the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: But we are talking about amendements to standing orders. Now, that is what is before the committee, and that is the matter which has been called.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I rise to what I think is a point of order. The Minister of National -Defence referred to a formal motion now before the committee with respect to amending standing order 9. I should like to ask him, or you, Mr. Chairman, when such a formal motion was made. As I understand it, the only motions which have been made with respect to this matter were motions made when Mr. Speaker was in the Chair: one made on March 7 by the Prime Minister that we go into committee of the whole to give consideration to this report, and a similar motion made to-day while Mr. Speaker was still in the Chair. I believe one of the reasons we are having so much difficulty is that we are simply considering a report without any
specific, formal motion before us. The only actual motion which was made to-day in committee was the one made by the hon. member for Temiscouata and which was ruled out of order. It seems to me that it would expedite matters if someone, preferably a private member I would say, were to move formally the adoption or the approval of the proposed amendment of standing order 9, so that we might get on. I rose to a point of order really to ask the Minister of National Defence if he would indicate when the formal motion to which he referred was made.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I do not know just what Hansard will show, but I distinctly heard, I think, the Chairman, after he took the Chair, use some such words as these, "The motion is that standing order 9 be amended" by doing so and so, and that is what I understood to be the item before the Chair. The Chairman can correct me if I am wrong.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Who made the motion?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: The motion, of course, would be called by the Chair and would be made by the Speaker. Let us check on that. The Chairman is here.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: The statement of the minister is correct.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: May I ask the Minister of National Defence a question the answer to which might clarify this deadlock? If the discussion should proceed on standing order 9, after general discussion of other items or amendments, and when those amendments or any of them should be accepted, would the report be accepted altogether, or would the latter part be accepted separately?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I understood that the agreement the other day was that we were to have the amendments to the standing orders put in order, in the form of separate amendments. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni objected to our talking about recommendations without identification, for instance "the recommendation in the middle of page so-and-so." He wanted them where they could be identified and separated; and as I understand it, we are dealing to-day with those amendments placed in that form. He has pointed out, quite properly, that they are not actually numbered, but they are in order, and can easily be identified as amendments of standing order so-and-so. My 'hon. friend has asked whether, if the amendment of standing order 9 is passed, that includes the passing of the so-called prologue or preamble. I take it that it does not, that it has nothing to do with the prologue or preamble, that the prologue or preamble has nothing to do with the
Rules of the House

amendment of standing orders as such; that, as each amendment is passed, the disposition of each one stands on its own feet. Consequently what emerges will be such amendments of standing orders in this book of parliamentary rules as are approved by this committee. There would therefore be no action by the committee approving these first two pages, which deals with certain general subjects and includes what the hon. member for Comox-Alberni calls "recommendations", but are really opinions and suggestions on two points of procedure in connection with handling the business of the house.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: May I ask if this procedure is not the accepting of the committee's report and if, in so doing, you certainly are not accepting or adopting the recommendations made by the committee? I rather agree with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni when he says that he does not want the preamble put in with standing order 9. If you look at page 2, regardless of what the Speaker has said in defining that word "recommendation", which he suggests should be changed to "suggestion"-I would point out that that has not been done yet-the report distinctly says "we therefore recommend". That is a recommendation. It goes on to say what the committee recommends. Taking the suggestion of the Minister of National Defence, that you include the preamble with the first amendment-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: No. I have not suggested that; I said you could talk about it.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I believe- it would expedite matters greatly if we would so arrange it as to vote on the preamble first, because there are recommendations there. If the chairman of the committee, who is the Speaker, wishes to change the word "recommendations" to "suggestions", that might alter the opinion of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni and of others as well who object to it. But if you accept this language as it stands, in the final analysis you are accepting the recommendations as laid down in the preamble. They are recommendations; there is no doubt about it. They may not be intended to be regarded as recommendations, and I take it from what the Speaker said a few moments ago that that is not the intention, that they are offered only as suggestions to the committee. But that does not alter the fact that as stated in the preamble they are recommendations. I suggest that we could solve the difficulty by taking the preamble first and disposing of it.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I take it that the report of the committee differs in no way from other reports submitted to the House of Commons, and until this committee adopts the report that is before us, the report does not become effective. We have the report before us at the present moment and we are now deliberating the question of changing the standing orders and rules of the house. We may either adopt or reject the amendments, but in our discussions we shall not be deliberating upon what has been called the preamble to the report.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I think I am correct in saying that the preamble is always the last portion of any measure that is passed, not the first. It simply means in this case that we do not reach the preamble but everyone will have expressed his opinion on it if he so desires. May I say this to the hon member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston). The last recommendation to which he refers is that:
When there is reason to believe that debate will be protracted, parties and groups recognized in the house shall confer and make arrangements either for alloting days or laying any plan for saving time whilst protecting freedom of speech for every representative of the people who sits in this house.
I ask my hon. friend, suppose the word "recommendation" were changed, would it make the slightest difference? The house is passing a resolution about something it cannot enforce. It is dealing entirely with a suggestion to the leaders of the various groups in the house with reference to conference, and it is really not an effective recommendation at all. It is a suggestion to those who have to do with the proceedings of the house that they may by compromise and convention make certain arrangements. I agree with the member for Comox-Alberni that the other is a little more definite. The recommendation is:
We therefore recommend that, when the yearly estimates have been brought down, one day a week be set aside for consideration of supply. If this is done, the house is not likely to find itself under the necessity of passing a great part of estimates in the dying days of the session.
-that is really a suggestion to the government, or whoever may be responsible for determining the day-to-day business of the house. It is not a suggestion to the committee.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Does the word "recommend" there mean something different from what it does on page 4, where it says, "The following amendments to standing orders are recommended"?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Perhaps the word there has the same meaning as in the context I have

Rules oj the House
quoted, but the point is that it is a recommendation to someone else. One recommendation is to the house, that we make certain amendments to the rules, and the other is to the government, that, in allocating days for business, they do certain things. My attention is called to the fact that in 1927 there was a similar committee sitting, and while the preamble of the report then submitted was very much more innocuous than this one, at the same time there were, however, one or two expressions indicating principles to which the committee had adhered and which might have been taken exception to by anyone who was then considering the report. I am instructed that the preamble to the report on that occasion simply treated as an introduction. It was not dealt with at all, and we find in volume 64 of the Journals of 1926-27 a tabulation setting out the amendments to the standing orders which were then dealt with, just as we have tabulated the amendments now proposed. The preamble itself, in the report of 1927, stated that the committee had agreed to certain amendments. I quote:
Your committe has adhered to the principle that the greatest freedom be allowed the house in both its debate and proceedings.
I am sure that someone could get up then and say that the committee had done no such thing.
Factors tending to restrict liberty have been eliminated.
That could have been made a controversial issue.
The tendency has been to reduce the number of standing orders and to make them clearer, with the object that only absolutely necessary rules be in force, so that the house will be more particularly guided by the general principles followed in British legislative assemblies and familiar to parliamentarians in Great Britain and the self-governing dominions.
That report was passed, not by dealing with the preamble but by dealing with the standing orders.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
There is apparently a great
deal of confusion in the minds of some hon. members on the question whether in the forepart of the report the intention is that what is stated shall be binding on the house or on the government as the case may be. I believe, however, that every member of the committee is clearly of the opinion that no such intention was contemplated when the report was drafted and framed. The whole intention was that it was a suggestion only and not a recommendation, and personally I cannot see how any possible amendment can be made. The first part of the report, as well as the evidence of the words in themselves, is clear that that was
only intended as a recommendation, or a suggestion or direction, if you like, to government as to certain matters in connection with the estimates, and also, in the second part, in connection with the rules and as regards the protraction of debates. I think I am speaking definitely the minds of the members of the committee when I say that this was a matter which they discussed and which they thought should be dealt with, but that they did not intend to make any revision of the standing orders for the purpose of giving effect to it. Their whole intention was that they should consider only the amendments which they felt they should submit to the house, and that is what I submit we should now deal with.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
May I make one last and no doubt futile effort to convince the government or the chairman as to the merits of this question. I do so in no spirit of antagonism to the government. Indeed, I wish to vote for one of these recommendations. I cannot understand however why the Speaker, the chairman of this committee, appears to be anxious to do the Charlie Chaplin act and disavow the paternity of his own baby. True, he may claim that it is not entirely his individual paternity, but he shares the responsibility with other members of the committee and now he appears like Charlie Chaplin to be hesitating and is anxious to repudiate paternity.
The report was brought into the house and, as the hon. member for Lincoln very truly says, it is obviously a report. The Speaker has made the suggestion that the word "recommend" in regard to the estimates is a general phrase; it is like the man who wrote a beautiful poem in regard to his regret over the mistakes of his lifetime, or perhaps even of the previous twenty-four hours, when he said something like this, "Flowers you might have sent, dear, are your haunting ghosts to-night." The Speaker seems to think this is a sort of academic thing which can be dismissed with his blessing in that way, but that is not the way in which it is brought into the house. This is what was said about it by the most astute constitutionalist in Canada, the Prime Minister, at page 1255 of Hansard for March 7:
We might well assume, I think, that so far as the first half of the report is concerned, if I may so designate it-
We seem to have a hard job defining it; one calls it a preamble, another calls it the first half; I think another called it an epilogue, and the next thing we know it will be a funeral oration.
-hon. members should not be committed too literally to all the statements which it sets forth, or to all its observations. They are
Rules of the House

general in nature, and in voting for or against the adoption of the report, if we are expected so to do, we might well, I think, be allowed to have certain mental reservations with regard to the adoption of all that appears there.
The Prime Minister wanted to have certain mental reservations, but some people object to that. They say, "We are going to vote on that on its merits, yes or no; we are not going to have a corner of our minds or hearts in which we believe something different from the way we vote." Now the Minister of Pensions and National Health comes along and says the best thing we can do is to forget about it. That would be. a very sad end to this report, which has been drawn up by some of the cleverest lawyers in the house; of the fourteen members of the committee I think nine were lawyers. Now we come down to the simple view. I am not opposing the report, but I want to discuss it. This matter can, I think, be settled in five minutes. The hon. gentleman who is leading the house tries to cover it up by saying that this does not really mean "recommendation" but that it means "suggestion", and I think one hon. member went so far as to say it was only a pious hope. It means just what it says; it is a recommendation. The word "recommend" on page 2 means exactly the same as it does on page 4, where we read:
The following amendments to the standing orders are recommended.
Get out of that if you can; say that in one place on page 2 it means nothing while in another place on page 4 it means everything. I cannot understand all this difficulty; all that is necessary is what I asked should be done the last time this matter was under discussion, that the recommendations should be put all together and numbered, so that we might vote on them one by one. To-day the leader of the government said he thought that had been done, but it has not, for two recommendations have been left out. The others have been grouped together so that we may understand them, but the first two recommendations have been omitted. Here we have eight or nine recommendations beginning on page 4, but the two recommendations contained on page 2 are not included. This can be settled very easily by putting at the top of the list of recommendations, or at the bottom -I do not care where they are-the two recommendations which are found on page 2. Is there anything wrong or anything difficult about that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
My hon. friend does not really mean that seriously, does he, in regard to the suggestion as to members of the groups

conferring? Surely he does not mean he wants to have the committee record its opinion about that.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I meant that it did not matter to me whether those two recommendations were at the head of the list or at the end of it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: But I am talking about the second recommendation. Does the hon. member really mean that he wants this recommendation put before this committee and solemnly passed upon?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: If I could stop that recommendation from going through I would stay here for a week or a fortnight. I think it is a thoroughly rotten recommendation, and I want to discuss it and vote it down.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Then why does the hon. gentleman bother with it?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I want it to be condemned-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Supposing it should be passed; it would be ineffective.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: -because only a short time ago the hon. gentleman himself made the suggestion that we should go on with the proposed amendment to standing order 9, and that when this amendment was adopted it would carry with it the first part of the report. I know he has now receded from that position, but I think Hansard will show that he took it a short time ago.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I really must be a little firm about this. My hon. friend will not find in what I said previously one syllable which could be interpreted in that way, and I have not receded from anything. I took my position in the beginning and I repeat it now, that the discussion can take place when we are considering the amendment to standing order 9, but that all we would vote on would be the amendment, and we can go on from there with the other amendments.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I accept the minister's statement; my opinion was different, but perhaps I was wrong, and I know the minister is a reputable gentleman. But supposing we put that recommendation back alongside the other one; it is only a pious hope thrown up to the government, who can do what they like about it. I do not want any pious resolutions like this put up to anybody; I do not want it to be left so that only parties and groups who are "recognized" in the house may confer. My hon. friends in the far corner will not be recognized. That is a definite thing; and perhaps two or three years from now the' ministry

Rules of the House
of the day would be perfectly justified in. saying, "We are going to put this into effect, because it was one of the recommendations made in writing by this committee." There is no question about that. If the thing is right let us pass it; if it is wrong let us vote it down.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I say it is just futile,

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I say once we get through discussing these amendments of the standing orders the debate will end. If anyone will give me a guarantee that nothing will be done along this line I shall be satisfied. I am not alone in this. I ami not in collaboration with anyone else, but I am quite sure I am voicing the wishes of many other hon. members when I say that we want an opportunity to support or turn down these specific things. Why not just include these two recommendations at the bottom of the list, and let us have every opportunity to express ourselves? We do not want to adopt the second recommendation; perchance we may want to adopt the first one, in regard to the estimates.
I am taking up a good deal of the time of the committee and I apologize, but I have not spoken very much this session; I ami not able to do so. I do not see why we could not be allowed to follow that course. Someone suggested that we might strike out the word "recommend" and insert the word "suggest". That might meet the difficulty in a way, but in a house of two hundred and forty-five intelligent people it is no use saying that "recommend" means one thing on one page and something different on another page. Now I have said all I am going to say; this discussion will have to go on, but time and history will show that I am right.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: As a member of the special committee I want to endorse what the Speaker has said. The committee did express certain opinions in the preamble, but they did not ask the house to make those opinions into rules. The only things we wanted to change were the standing orders.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: You did not say so.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I hope my hon. friend will let me have a moment in which to say a few words. I am trying to express my opinion, speaking with my knowledge as a member of that committee. While these opinions were expressed, it was not intended that they should become standing orders. If we expressed the opinion that in order to facilitate the business of this house it would be a splendid thing for the different groups to get together, that does not mean that it should be made a rule or anything of the kind; that is only an expression of opinion. I think the matter was put
very clearly by the Speaker and by the hon. member for New Westminster. We did give a good deal of attention to the recommendations we made, and hon. members are at liberty to adopt or reject them, as the case may be. Perhaps we were not unanimous in regard to everything, but we were fairly unanimous on the recommendations we have made in regard to amendments of standing orders. As to the opinions expressed in the preamble, however, we did not ask that they be translated into rules of the house, and I think hon. members generally understand that. Surely that point has been explained now; it was dealt with by the acting leader of the government as well.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I think we should try to find some way to break this deadlock and get on with our business. I hesitate to disagree with the hon. member for Comox-Albemi, for whose parliamentary acumen and experience I have the greatest regard. But I do insist that he is wrong in his attitude toward this report. As a matter of fact the report is clear, as is also the intention of the committee. It made certain recommendations respecting the standing orders of the house. Those recommendations are definitely stated. Then the committee suggested that other things might be done, but it did not include those as changes or amendments of standing orders. The committee had the same power in regard to those matters as it had in regard to the standing orders for which it seeks amendments.
It would seem that the first recommendation on page 2 has caused much of the discussion. Before that suggestion was made the committee said this:
Your committee does not think it would be advisable to change the present system-
That is, the present standing order.
-and it believes that the elasticity of the present rules makes it possible to apply them in new situations from time to time.
This makes it quite clear that the committee did not wish to change the standing order in regard to estimates. Had it wished to do so it would have offered the amendment among the other recommendations found on the following pages. The committee felt, however, that the government in dealing with the business of the house might make certain changes which would facilitate that business and give better satisfaction to hon. members.
The committee has said:
We, however, desire to submit that considerable time could be saved if the committee of supply sat oftener in the early part of the session.
That deals with the point I have mentioned.
Rules of the House

We now come to the suggestion in the next paragraph, found in these words:
We have recommended a few amendments but we feel that this house cannot go further in regulating its discussions.
Feeling that way, we are not offering any amendments in that regard.
Then the introduction goes on to say:
In spite of limitations now existing, every resolution and bill is given ample opportunities for debate in committee of the whole, standing and select committees and on the second and third reading; but as the allotment of days, under a special rule, might prevent members from speaking, it should not be ordered under the authority of a standing order.
Consequently the committee is not making that recommendation. But it is suggesting that the government consider facilitating business by holding consultations with leaders of other groups in the house. That is all the committee has done in that connection.
I suggest that we deal with the amendments of the standing order. If any other member wishes to have a standing order in respect of those two suggestions, I believe the rules of the house would allow that the amendments be made. I do believe, however, that it is this sort of futile discussion which brings parliamentary institutions into disrepute.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I believe if this committee were to meet again it would have another amendment to offer, in view of our having spent two hours on the discussion thus far. However, as I see it, the purpose of the committtee was to bring about a condition whereby the business of the house might be carried on more efficiently.
I have two suggestions to make. Some years ago I presented a petition to a former minister of public works in which we pointed out that some way should be found whereby hon. members occupying seats in far comers of the house would not have to leave their seats and move to other places in the house in order to hear. It is difficult to hear in this chamber. We note that four seats are reserved for the debates reporters. Why would those four seats be set aside in the centre of the chamber, if it were possible to hear with ease?
Why do we come to parliament? Do we not come to listen to and to take part in debates? Unless one has a strong voice, it is impossible for another member in a far corner to hear what is being said. I believe the Minister of Public Works and his staff should find some way to facilitate the hearing of speeches. People in the gallery would like to hear, too-especially those in the press gallery.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: And especially when you speak.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
This afternoon the leader of the opposition could not be heard by members of the C.C.F. When the matter was called to his attention he had to turn his face away from the Chair, with the result that the Chair could not hear him. Surely this matter should be considered.
I made a suggestion a while ago that the doors should be opened before Mr. Speaker proceeds to open the day's sitting. I believe this would be a good thing, and for this reason: All those who, through courtesy, come to hear the proceedings of the house would see how the sitting is opened. They would see, too, that the House of Commons stands upon a solid foundation. When Mr. Speaker, in a petition from the prayer says, "May Thy Kingdom come", it is clear that members in all parts of the house, through Mr. Speaker, are really pledging themselves to work for the kingdom of heaven to come on earth. Surely the general public should know this. If it is good for a few members of the house to come here and silently worship the Almighty, then I say it would be good for the general public. And it is in keeping with the statement of Him who gave us that prayer, when He said, "Whosoever will may come."
Some have urged that freedom of speech has been curtailed. I fail to understand that position, because I have been able to find lots of opportunity for anything I have had to say. Since I have come to the house I have found no minister, no whip, or anybody else who has attempted to curtail my remarks. I am going to think for myself and vote as I like.
Further, in respect of standing order 9 it is my view that no member should sit in the house and refuse to vote. Why is the member here? Surely he or she should be prepared to take sides, if they have any convictions whatever. Certainly I support that amendment.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I shall take only a very few minutes to make my contribution to the confusion which apparently already exists.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: And add a little more.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
It is clear that this general discussion is precipitated because of the introductory material in the report. Most hon. members feel that by adopting the report they will at the same time approve the suggestions or recommendations made by the committee in that introductory material. I would ask Mr. Chairman to indicate, if he will, just how or when we shall register our approval or disapproval of the introductory part of the report? Shall we by adopting the first amendment at the same time approve the recommendations or suggestions or, when we

Rules oj the House
have finished with the specific recommendation, shall we then be asked to adopt the report as amended? Is there any place in the procedure where we shall be asked to approve the introductory material in this report? Personally I should like to see that opportunity offered. There are a number of suggestions in the introductory part of the report that in my opinion, if followed by the government, will improve the procedure in the house. Would the Chairman indicate if there will be an opportunity of approving by vote the introductory part of this report?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: The committee is asked to approve the report of the committee for the amendment of the rules of the house. At the present moment we are dealing with the proposed changes and amendments to the rules and proceedings of the House of Commons. That will be the final report as far as the committee of the whole is concerned.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I have waited now for nearly two hours for the point to be decided as to what the procedure shall be. I have listened intently to the proceedings so far. If we as a committee are not able to determine the procedure by which we shall attempt to improve the procedure of the house then I say we are in a very bad way indeed. I think the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver East might properly be emphasized at this time. The public fail to understand proceedings of the kind that have taken place this afternoon in this chamber; such proceedings tend to throw a shadow of disrepute in the minds of some people on the proceedings of this house, and parliament to some extent becomes a bit of a laughing stock to the people who do not understand the general situation as it exists.
As I understand it, we are dealing with a report of a committee. If we depart from that and get into a discussion on a number of items in connection with the report, then I think we are departing from what we should be doing. I suggest that regardless of the discussion this afternoon, we should decide finally to deal with the report as such. Let us go on with the general discussion as I suggested in the first instance. Let us deal with the first part of the report, thereby having an opportunity to deal with the two recommendations which the hon. member for Comox-Alberni suggested. Let us get that out of the way. Surely that is a short-cut to all of this. Let us decide one way or the other about it and then let us go on to the particular items. I find that the introduction is included in the conclusion of the report as well. That shows the extent to which we have gone in completely confusing the whole issue before the
committee. I have some things I should like to say in a general way about the matter of house procedure, but I have been unable to do so because the procedure has not yet been determined.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Perhaps I did not make myself very clear. I have tried to trace a line of conduct in the present discussion. We all realize that this is not a bill. It is something like the war appropriation bill where wide latitude is given. I think I have gathered the consensus of the members of this committee. At the beginning wide latitude was given to the discussion. I have ruled that there is no preamble. We are dealing with a matter that touches on the freedom of parliament and parliamentarians. I thought I should allow the discussion to be fairly general. I agree with the leader of the opposition. I hope we shall now come to the first amendment that is before the committee. Going back to the introduction, there is a schedule to the report. As far as a preamble is concerned, we may call it that or anything else, but I have nothing of that kind before me. Standing order 76 reads as follows:
In proceedings in committee of the whole house upon bills, the preamble is first postponed, and then every clause considered by the committee in its proper order; the preamble and title to be last considered.
This is not a bill. I must leave it in the hands of the members of the committee of the whole. I thought I should give a lead in the general discussion and then go on to the passing of the proposed amendments.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
It seems surprising that the members of the house now in committee of the whole should be so much exercised about the introductory remarks that the committee submitted in its report on the amendment to the standing orders and rules. The introduction is headed as a commentary on parliamentary procedure, reviewing in general parliamentary procedure as we have it here in this house and making some suggestions and perhaps unfortunately using the words: "We recommend". The committee did not go so far as to offer any specific amendment of any standing order to carry out a recommendation. It will He entirely with the house and with the government as to whether they go farther than to adopt or not to adopt the specific amendments of certain standing orders which the committee recommend. There are 121 standing orders governing the house. After a number of meetings of the committee it was decided to offer amendments to only ten of the standing orders. These are the amendments that were offered.
Rules of the House

They appear in the report, ten in all. I submit that if these amendments are considered and adopted or defeated, then there is no necessity of adopting the preamble to the report or the introduction to the report. It stands merely as a general representation to the house. It does not profess to bind the house at all. There is no motion before the committee that the report be adopted. As I understand it, the motion now before the committee is that the suggested amendments to standing order 9 be adopted. That is what we are considering. That is what we should do or refuse to do. Having done that, we should then go on to the next one, which is No. 11. The committee may never be called upon to adopt the introduction. There is no reason why they should. It stands merely as a record of the opinion of this committee and the committee does not ask the committee of the whole to deal with it at all. It asks the committee of the whole to deal merely with the specific amendments that have been suggested.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I thoroughly agree with every word said by the hon. member for Yukon. His statements will be confirmed if we look at the terms of reference to this committee which may be found in Votes and Proceedings of this house of Tuesday, February 1, 1944. The reference is as follows:
Mr. Mackenzie King, seconded by Mr. Ilsley, moved,-That a special committee consisting of Messrs. Black (Yukon), Fauteaux, Golding, Hanson (York-Sunbury), Isnor, Mackenzie (Vancouver Centre), Maclnnis, Mcllraith, Maybamk, St. Laurent and Quelch, be appointed to assist Mr. Speaker in revising the standing orders of the house with a view to simplify, accelerate and expedite its business, and to report to the house during the present session.
Therefore the contention of the hon. member for Yukon is absolutely correct. We are concerned only with the terms of the reference which calls for an inquiry into a revision of the standing orders, and that the said committee report to the house during the present session. I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, with the consent of the committee, that we should now proceed to discuss these revisions in detail.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
The first thing to do is to know what is before us. There has been some conflict of opinion regarding what is called in different ways the expression of the opinion of the members of the committee. I have the Votes and Proceedings of February 1 containing the order of reference which states that that committee should be appointed to assist Mr. Speaker in revising the standing orders of the house with a view to simplify,
("Mr. George Black.]
accelerate and expedite the business and to report to the house in the present session. The reason why there was the misunderstanding is not due to what has been said by the hon. members here. It is precisely because the report has to be put in the hands of Mr. Chairman. That is the first mistake. A report that comes from a special committee cannot be amended except by the committee of the whole house itself. That is the way it is done; it cannot be done otherwise, and even if some sheets of paper are not before you, Mr. Chairman, it does not mean that the full report of the special committee is not before you. That is as clear as crystal.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I have rendered my decision. There is a way of appealing from my decision. I rule this discussion out of order, because there is no preamble before the Chair.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
That is all right, but if there is no preamble there is an introduction which I have in my hand. But leaving that aside, if the first three pages are the basis for the proposed amendments, we must know what they contain, and they contain a series of contradictions and of errors in constitutional law. They contain some errors that a first-year student in constitutional law would detect. Let us see what is the basis of these proposed amendments. The report says:
Your committee, in the performance of the important duty assigned to it by the house, has taken into account the existence of general criticism of parliament both by members and representative citizens.
That I deny. The second sentence reads:
It has fully realized that much is expected of the House of Commons where the views of the people are finding expression and where industrial and economic conditions are demanding parliamentary attention and solution.
That is insignificant. It goes on:
The main question before the committee was whether procedure should be amended so that the house may be able to do more legislative work in the time at its disposal and increase its efficiency as a critical and controlling assembly.	.
The work that we do here does not depend upon the rules of the house but upon the legislation that is submitted to us by the government. If, for instance, the selective service " legislation had been submitted to parliament instead of being passed by order in council it would have been much better and it would have shown a p-roper deference to parliament, much more than the amendments to the rules now proposed. Again the report says:
Criticisms of parliament seem to have been inadequately considered in relation to the whole structure of parliament-

Rules of the House
Imagine, criticism in regard to the whole structure of parliament!
-the necessary party system and the complex situation created by a war which is now in its fifth year.
Everybody knows that. It goes on:
These criticisms arise from opinions concerning the functions of parliament which are often based upon such misconceptions as the view that parliament is primarily a board of directors with the members of the cabinet as its executive staff, and that members, instead of endeavouring to reconcile as much as possible all the elements of public opinion, which is difficult in our diversified country, should rigidly consider every question on its own exclusive merits.
That is insignificant.
Suc-h, however, is not the true function of a legislative body composed of 245 members elected to discuss the management of public affairs.
Here is what I find wrong in this introduction. I find voices of good and voices of evil. There are some statements in these three pages that are absolutely true and some that are absolutely wrong, and when something is partly good and partly bad, I consider it all bad and I want to get rid of it. That is my point of view. It goes on:
Debates may sometimes be lengthy but they bring home to the administration the advisability or unpopularity of a particular line of policy and they must -be heard because democratic government rests upon public opinion.
That is true.
Parliament is the assembly of representatives elected by the people where great issues are debated, or should be debated;-
That again is true.

it is not primarily a body of auditors charged with the inspection of departmental accounts.
That is false. It is one of the principles of the British North America Act that parliament should have a check on expenditures. It is our duty to look into the expenditures of this country and to have its accounts before us. We are not auditors, but we have that right, which was won after a constitutional fight by our forefathers. Therefore I say that that statement is absolutely false.
Freedom of speech is one of the inalienable privileges of members of the House of Commons.
True.
It is in truth the privilege of their constituents and it is secured to members not for their personal benefit but to enable them to discharge the functions of their office.
The second part of that is true, but the first part of the sentence is partly true and partly false. It says:
It is in truth the privilege of their constituents. . . .
It is not the constituents who sit here. We sit here as the representatives of our constituents, and we have the right to discuss all matters pertaining to their welfare. It goes on:
Without it, the essence of the country's liberty * does not exist.
That is true.
The present procedure was devised to reflect the freedom of all the members of the house, but we must realize that in war time parliament is bound to divest itself of some of its prerogatives in order to strengthen the government's power.
That is wrong, and it is in contradiction with the first part which says that the rules are amended to increase the efficiency of parliament. How can anyone reconcile those two statements? On the one hand it says it is to strengthen the power of parliament, and on the other hand it is to give our legal powers to the government. Most absurd, most wrong -total ignorance of parliamentary rights and of the constitution. It goes on:
The principle of majority rule is a constitutional convention upon which all British parliamentary government is built-
True.
-but this must collapse in proportion as the principle of the protection of minorities begins to decay.
What is the meaning of that sentence? It is so foggy, so impossible to understand, that it should be explained. It is most foolish. It goes on:
Rules are not sufficient to preserve freedom of speech and to uphold the dignity of the House of Commons.
I admit it, and for this reason, that practice counts for more than rules.
Standing orders depend for their success upon the prevalence of good will amongst all members who have to work under them.
A member-he was an old member too- once asked me what the standing orders were. I told him they were the rules of the house. He said, "Thank you." He did not even know what they were. The first thing is to read the standing orders and try to understand them. They are not so bad, after all, although they were mutilated a little over fifteen years ago.
Standing orders depend for their success upon the prevalence of good will amongst all members who have to work under them.
That is true, but they depend for their success upon the rulings of the chair, and some of the rulings that were given some years ago were most unjust. I shall not recall them now because they are in the minds of all members. The chairman must know the rules and apply them according to their spirit. That
Rules oj the House

was not done for some time when another speaker was in the chair and when another chairman was occupying the chair here.
The house must rely on the forbearance of its members and on the general acquiescence in the enforcement by the Speaker of the rule which requires that members should strictly confine, themselves to matters immediately pertinent to the subject of debate.
That is true but the rule is there already. What is the use of repeating the same thing? It is useless redundance. It goes on:
In a report presented to the United Kingdom House of Commons in 1931, the following statement appears:	"Your committee would
urge that unless understanding and a common loyalty prevail there will be a danger of the collapse of the system of representative government ... if the principles of equality among members, publicity of the house's proceedings..."
Publicity of the house's proceedings! How is it that members of the wartime information board go around to the press with scissors, telling them not to publish this and that which hon. members have said? I am not making complaint of the two agencies, the Canadian Press and the British United Press, but there are those who do not want these reports to be published, and who do mutilate them, and it is these very gentlemen who complain afterwards that members are not doing their duty. Let them inform first their readers of what we are doing. Afterwards they will be in a position to criticize what we have done, and their readers will be sufficiently informed to give a fair judgment.
. . freedom of speech, majority rule, or the right of the minority to an adequate expression of opinion are consciously challenged, there is an indication of some serious defect in the life of the nation. . ."
That is true, sir. If there is no freedom of speech in the house, there is an indication of some serious defect in the life of the nation. It was said in England, but it is just as true here as it is true in England:
"These larger considerations cannot .be regulated by rules and orders:	they are the
responsibility of each member of the house."
They are the responsibility of the Chair, and they are our responsibility, as a body of men who have to maintain our traditional liberties. The report continues:
Your committee, in all its deliberations, has kept m mind the importance of not impairing the rights of minorities.
That is right. I agree with that.
Two fundamental principles govern the procedure of the house. They are, that the government shall, so long as it can maintain a majority, be able to secure such legal powers as it considers necessary for administration, . . .
That is absolutely wrong. Where does the government have legal powers? Anyone can
fMr. Pouliot.]
look in the constitution and ascertain that the government has no legal powers; it has only executive powers. It is against this kind of thing in the report that I protest. Why should we abandon our rights to the government? We have rights here. We have the right to check legislation, and to do so at each one of the readings of a bill. Why should we abandon our rights as a parliament? This is the kind of thing in this report which I find absolutely wrong and despicable.
The report goes on to say that it is a fundamental principle-
. . . that minorities, however small, shall be able to criticize that administration.
That is all right, but let us see how it works. In the first place is asserted something which is absolutely false, which is absolutely opposed to the constitution, and in the second place it is commended as giving a chance to the minority. "I give you poison, but it is for your good; it will make you strong. I will kill you, but it is to send you to heaven."
Standing orders must protect them, and it is all the more important that they be founded on right and justice because they are merely resolutions of the house whicfi can be swept away by a majority vote.
"Founded on right and justice"! I do not suppose anybody thinks we can change the constitution.
Your committee is of the firm opinion that these rights cannot be alienated even if the house, in maintaining them, may protract sessions and lay itself open to severe criticism.
In saying that, the committee does well.
The suggestion that estimates should be referred to standing or select committees has been given earnest consideration and carefully reviewed. It strikes at the root of ministerial responsibility and it divests members of the privilege of criticizing from the floor of the house without advice, suggestion or influence of any kind, all departmental expenditures submitted by the government. No proposals subversive of this settled rule of action can be safely embodied in any scheme for securing closer parliamentary control. One of the objections to this proposal is that if all the estimates are referred to a standing or select committee the motion for the Speaker to leave the chair shall be abolished, which means fewer opportunities for private members to move amendments setting forth grievances or expressing want of confidence in the government.
Reading that, one would suppose that everything is done to give hon. members more liberty, more freedom of speech than we have now; yet there come the scissors, "cut the speech, cut the speech, cut the speech," all the time. I think it is hypocrisy to say one thing and do another. Anyone reading the preamble would gain the impression that the object is to give hon. members the fullest and most perfect freedom of speech; yet we

Rules oj the House
know that members cannot speak here, they cannot speak there; more members must rise in the case of an appeal; but all this is said to be for their own good and for the strengthening of parliamentary institutions, to allow members to say anything they like, and to protect minorities. That is the way it is done. If to sustain charges, more members must rise, it is for the protection of minorities! The number required to appeal from Mr. Speaker's rulings must be twenty instead of five, but it is to protect minorities! And so forth and so on.
One of t.he objections to this proposal is that if all the estimates are referred to a standing or select committee the motion for the Speaker to leave the chair shall be abolished, which means fewer opportunities for private members to move amendments setting forth grievances or expressing want of confidence in the government. The procedure required to keep _ this privilege unimpaired would reduce the efficiency of the committee's functions and it would be so involved as to be misunderstood and hard to enforce. Certain estimates may be^ occasionally referred to a select committee in order to ascertain facts which the house desires to know, but this practice should be adopted guardedly and only in very special circumstances. Your committee does not think it would be advisable to change the present system and it believes that the elasticity of the present rules makes it possible to apply them in new situations from time to time.
Here we have it.
We, however, desire to submit that considerable time could be saved if the committee of supply sat oftener in the early part of the session.
We do not need rules for that. Everything is in the hands of the government. When they want to submit estimates it is up to them to do so. We do not need rules for that, although such a rule would not be any more absurd than standing order 12, paragraph 4:
No member may pass between the chair and the table, nor between the chair and the mace when the mace has been taken off the table by the sergeant-at-arms.
"The chair" is the chair in which Mr. Chairman sits. How can anyone pass between Mr. Chairman's chair and the mace? And there are other things which are unbelievable. Standing order 5 states:
Every member is bound to attend the service of the house, unless leave of absence has been given him by the house.
What hon. member indicates with his fingers that he wishes to obtain the leave of the house to dictate his correspondence or attend a committee? That is a rule of the house which is not observed. What is the good of having rules which will never be observed? They should be stricken off the record; they are obsolete.
To return to the committee's report:
We therefore recommend that, when the yearly estimates have been brought down, one day a week be set aside for consideration of supply. If this is done, the house is not likely to find itself under the necessity of passing a great part of the estimtaes in the dying days of the session.
This is the recommendation which I am precluded from discussing on its merits because it is not supposed to be before Mr. Chairman now, as he told me that he had ruled.
The allotment of a certain number of days for the debates which appear to become protracted was considered Your committee was averse to multiplying rules of this character. There are already several restrictions which have been found necessary for parliamentary work and which are accepted in almost every elected assembly.
Not in England. Are they accepted everywhere except in England? Not everywhere; in only a few dominions.
