speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: The ruling I had given was that we have no preamble before the committee at the present time. I assumed it would be very hard to stop hon. members from what might be called a general discussion.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I will tell the leader of the house that I am reading it so that it may be on record, so that those who see Hansard to-morrow will know what we have been discussing and that we have been fighting for the cause of liberty, for freedom of speech. That is what I want. If the hon. gentleman will permit me, I was saying that there is something of a paradox in these pages. The suggestion is being made that the House of Commons should divest itself of its legal powers in favour of the government and against the constitution itself, and I deny that we have the right to do that. That is the suggestion that is twice repeated in these incredible pages. I continue:
We have recommended a few amendments but we feel that this house cannot go further in regulating its discussions. In spite of limitations now existing, every resolution and bill is
Rules of the House

given ample opportunities for debate in committee of the whole, standing and select committees and on the second and third readings; but as the allotment of days, under a special rule, might prevent members from speaking, it should not be ordered under the authority of a standing order.
It is just to give an opportunity to members to speak; it is not to prevent them from being able to speak that their speeches are curtailed. Most incredible!
Your committee is not prepared to recommend such an innovation in our procedure which must be adapted to our own conditions and be thoroughly Canadian.
Here it is, "Canadian". If it were truly Canadian it would be better.
Our recommendation is that, when there is reason to believe that debate will be protracted, parties and groups recognized in the house shall confer and make arrangements cither for allotting days or laying any plan for saving time whilst protecting freedom of speech for every representative of the people who sits in this house.
Once again the voices of good and evil. These gentlemen will meet together in the most undemocratic fashion and decide that private members have not the right to speak.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: They do it.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: They may do it but it is a shame that it is done.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: They do it now.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I know they do, but I have always protested against it. I do not see why any member who is the leader of a group should have any more rights than a private member who is a back-bencher. That is my point. In the house we are all equals. The Prime Minister said so in 1926. He said he was the first among equals, and he said something to that effect not long ago. It is not disrespect for any one to point this out. If anyone sits here he does so in his capacity as a member of the House of Commons. If someone is elected grand commander of the illustrious and noble order of such-and-such, that does not give him any right to sit in the House of Commons. He sits here because he is a member of parliament, and all members of parliament have the same rights. I do not see, therefore, how any men belonging to any party or group may join together to prevent any member from saying what he has a right to say. It is most undemocratic, most despotic, most dictatorial.
Your committee _ did not think it advisable to take up at this time the question of the alleged suppression of initiative on the part of the private member.
[Mr. Pouliot.l
Here again is the voice of good.
As the nation has been at war for over four years-
It was supposed to be five years, here it is only four years. The more we read, the less we are at war.
-and government business has been given precedence over private members' motions and bills, this is not the proper session to consider that part of our procedure.
I do not insist.
Conditions prevailing in war time are such that private members notices of motions and private bills must give way to war measures.
I am willing to agree to that.
The order of business followed since 1940 has been based on resolutions which practically abolish private members' days. It is an exceptional situation and perhaps the house had better wait until normal conditions return before the private member's place in the house can be considered.
I believe that the private member's place in the house must be considered in all discussions of public affairs, and if for the duration of the war we give precedence to government business I do not see why the rights of private members should be curtailed in debate.
Rules of practice are necessary in the House of Commons as well as in any court of justice and other public institutions, but the multiplicity of standing orders dealing with the basic principles of parliamentary procedure ought not to be encouraged.
That is why I am against having new rules. I find this statement very timely. We should not have more rules. I am against new rules. Here we have something good and something bad, something bad and something good-it is like an orange. Take an orange, part of which is rotten.; will you eat it? No; you will throw it away. The orange that I hold in my hand has something good in it, but most of it is bad, and that is why I want to throw it into the waste-paper basket, as I did the famous Purvis report on unemployment. To continue:
There were no standing orders relating to public business in the United Kingdom House of Commons until 1707, and there were only three from 1715 to 1821-over a century. There are ninety-five to-day. We have 81, besides 10 dealing with the staff and 28 governing the library of parliament. Your committee is aware that members of this house are reluctant to impose restrictions on their freedom and independence, and that any attempt to translate procedure into precise rules will deprive them of the very quality which render them adaptable to new and varying conditions, or unusual combinations of circumstances, and might have the effect of restricting rather than safeguarding their privileges.
Amen. Then, there is another paragraph. It was said that members had been asked to express views about the matter. That is the

Rules of the House
part I object to because it leaves those who read it under a false impression, that the purpose of these regulations is to give more latitude to the members when,, in fact, as I understand it, it deprives them of all rights they have now. The leader of the opposition has to defend his own move, because he himself suggested changing the rules. He did not know what he was speaking about when he mentioned a certain matter to the house, and I told him that the first thing to do in connection with the public accounts committee was to lay a charge and ask for a sitting of the committee on a specified charge. And then he went on with it. It has become a Bracken slogan, that we must reform the rules of the house. Was it not his intention to depreciate members to your right, Mr. Chairman, so that they could be easily defeated at the next election? To me, it was a political move. That was the intention, to depreciate the majority of the house in order to have an easy success at the next election. And then we went on. Who had a diary to get in touch with editors at various intervals? It is time enough to write another article to remind the Prime Minister and the cabinet that the rules of the house should be changed. We had certain views periodically expressed by the man with a diary. He must have had connections in Montreal and Ottawa, in Toronto and in Winnipeg, and perhaps in the press gallery. When will he write another editorial about the. change in the rules of the house.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, throughout the afternoon session we were dealing with the proposed amendments to the standing orders, but to my mind we made very little progress. I agree with the point of view expressed by the hon. member for Yukon, a former Speaker of this house, and supported by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre. I view the first three pages of this report as explanatory notes outlining the opinions of the committee upon certain aspects of the rules governing the procedure of this house, and even if the whole report should be adopted I cannot see that what is contained in these three pages would in any way amend any of the standing orders.
Throughout the discussion it has appeared to me that the emphasis has been placed upon the necessity of protecting the rights 100-148
and privileges of private members of parliament. I would be the last to support any suggestion which I thought might violate the rights or the independence of hon. members, but I do think that in this chamber we should not overlook the fact that if we are to maintain that high prestige which should be maintained with respect to free, democratic parliaments, we must keep in mind the necessity of so regulating the business of parliament as to expedite the important and essential matters which come up for consideration. In this discussion I think too little emphasis has been placed upon that important feature. I am not unmindful of the fact that in many countries democratic parliaments have disappeared as a means of government; nor am I unmindful of the fact that what has been substituted for those democratic institutions has eliminated to a very large extent not only the independence of elected representatives of the people but also the rights of individual citizens. Something has been said with respect to free speech. I believe the parliament at Westminster is the citadel of freedom of speech; and that brings me to a thought which is expressed at the bottom of page 2 of this report, in these words:
Our recommendation is that, when there is reason to believe that debate will be protracted, parties and groups recognized in the house shall confer and make arrangements either for allotting days or laying any plan for saving time whilst protecting freedom of speech for every representative of the people who sits in this house.
As far as I am concerned, as I said in a debate last year, the parliament at Westminster adopted the principle of the allocation of time as applied to the consideration of bills, estimates and other business of the house. I have not altered my opinion; I am still in favour of the adoption by this house of the principle of the allocation of time, but after fully considering the matter the committee decided that this was not an opor-tune time to recommend to the house the amendment of our standing orders to bring that regulation into effect. I am quite prepared to go on and discuss these other amendments and not press that matter at the moment, but I want to make one point clear. I am quite sure that the adoption of the principle of the allocation of time by the parliament at Westminster has neither violated nor destroyed freedom of speech in that citadel, where the importance of freedom of speech is considered as great as in any other part of the globe. In view of the fact that they adopted that principle as far back as the early eighteen-eighties, I am sure we might well give consideration to following their example. In the meantime, I do not

Rules of the House

see why we could not dispense with this endless discussion on the foreword, and get down to the discussion of the amendments to the standing orders as they are listed in this report beginning with standing order 9 on page 4.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I wish to register my protest against the proposed amendment to standing order 9, which reads:
And every member present in the chamber when the question is finally put iby Mr. Speaker shall be obliged to vote, and if he does not vote Mr. Speaker shall call upon him to_ vote and his name shall be recorded accordingly. If he persists in not voting he may be named by Mr. Speaker for having violated a standing order of the house.
What is the purpose of this amendment? When the Prime Minister moved the resolution setting up the committee he expressed himself in these words:
That a special committee ... be appointed to assist Mr. Speaker in revising the standing orders of the house with a view to simplify, accelerate and expedite its business, and to report to the house during the present session.
Can anyone tell me how this amendment will help to simplify, accelerate and expedite the business of the house? This was the purpose of the appointment of the committee. The first amendment is to oblige a man sitting in the house to register his vote. I do not see any reason to support any such amendment. In the Votes and Proceedings of March 3, there were some explanatory notes as to the amendments. It is said that the practice for many years was that a member who remained seated during a division was often required by Mr. Speaker to declare on which side he voted. I have sat in the house since 1925, and my recollection is clear with respect to 1931, in which year on the occasion of a vote a few members remained seated in the house, and did not register their votes. In that year Mr. Speaker did not render a decision; as a matter of fact he refused to intervene.
Then on April 28, 1931, Mr. Bourassa moved a motion, seconded by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) that the standing orders of the house be amended by inserting the direction that upon a division a member is not obliged to vote. As a matter of fact, later on a committee was appointed, on the initiative of the then Prime Minister, Mr. Bennett. A special committee was set up to consider amendments to the standing orders of the house governing procedure to be followed in taking a division. I do not know that any report was made. But that was the only occasion I recall when members were challenged to register their votes.

In the explanatory notes to which I referred a moment ago it is pointed out that in 1906, in the United Kingdom house, a standing order was passed relieving members of the obligation to vote. Certainly the practice in the United Kingdom cannot be held out as an argument in favour of this amendment, because over there members are not obliged to vote, or register their votes. I am trying to find a single reason which might lead me to support the amendment. In the preamble -some call it a preamble, while others say it is not a preamble-there is reference to freedom of members. Well, when a member is entitled to sit in the house he is entitled to his seat all the time deliberations of the house are in progress. He is entitled either to listen or not to listen to the debates. Some members may read their newspapers-as they are now doing. No one objects to their doing so. They can participate in the debate, or refrain from doing so, and no one will object. They are at liberty to do as they wish in that regard. When a division is taken, should a member be obliged to register his vote for or against a motion?
There are many inconveniences connected with a rule of that kind. For instance, with respect to the speech from the throne at the present session we know there was a main motion, an amendment and a subamendment. Members were called upon to register their votes on that division. If an hon. member did not want to vote on the subamendment, he could not have stayed in the house. He would have had to leave. What would have happened? Mr. Speaker read the main motion, the amendment and the subamendment, and then said that we would vote on the subamendment. As soon as the vote was taken on the subamendment, the amendment was voted on, without reading the amendment again or, in fact without reading anything, and without ringing the house bells. If a member did not want to vote on the subamendment, but wanted to vote on the amendment, he could not have registered his vote. He would have been outside the house, and would not have known when to come in. Surely that is an inconvenience.
Sometimes a member may agree with part of a motion, and disagree with part of it. If he votes for the motion, then he is registering his approval of everything contained in it. On the other hand, if he votes against it, he is registering his disapproval of the whole motion. The only alternative is to abstain from voting. Possibly that is why in England they have passed the standing order to which I referred a moment ago by which members

Rules of the House
were relieved of the obligation to vote and, if they wished, could remain at their seats.
I shall not detain the committee longer. My submission is that the committee was not appointed to propose such an amendment as this, that there are no arguments which could be offered in favour of it, and that on the other hand there are many which could be urged against it.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the subject we are discussing is the amendment to standing order 9. If it were not for the fact that the amendment may come to a vote, and no amendment to the amendment is permitted, I would be inclined to move an amendment to proposed new standing order. I say that because, first of all I am opposed to compelling a member to vote. I can see no good reason why a member of the House of Commons cannot sit in his place and, if he feels he should not vote, be permitted to remain seated, without being forced to leave the chamber. If the matter is to be cleared up so that a member can do so, then I think some note should be taken of citation 69 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, second edition. And, by the way, referring to voting in the House of Commons may I point out that there are some twenty-two citations dealing with standing order 9. However, citation 69 at page 25 reads:
69. Under ancient custom, refusal to vote was considered a serious parliamentary offence, hut the practice was changed in 1906 by the British House adopting a standing order whereby a member is not obliged to vote. That standing order does not apply to the Canadian Commons. The practice has not been changed in Canada where every member *who has heard the question put is bound to vote.
So that, if we want to clarify it, that is if it is the unanimous opinion of the committee that a member should be allowed to remain seated in the .House of Commons and not be compelled to leave, as is the custom in other parliaments, then I suggest that citation 69 be looked up. Apparently there is still doubt in the minds of the Speaker and other hon. members as to whether a member should be compelled to register his vote.
I remember I think it was 1931, when Henri Bourassa was nearly named by the Speaker. The Speaker of that date, the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black), called upon Mr. Bourassa to say which way he intended to vote. For about half an hour things were very tense in the house, as I might tell hon. members who were hot there at that time, because the Speaker was about to name him, upon which he would be supposedly sent to the tower but actually, I suppose, it would have been to the Chateau Laurier, where he 100-1481
would have been well looked after. Under the rules he could have been named by the Speaker and, if named, he would have been escorted from the chamber. After some argument the request was withdrawn, but that provision is still in our rules. To my mind it should be completely clarified.
I am against forcing an hon. member to say whether he will vote. When a vote is taken our names appear on Hansard as a record for the people of our constituencies and the rest of the country to see. If an hon. member does not vote, his name is not there. We have the protection of Hansard to show whether an hon. member voted. Personally I cannot see why an hon. member should be compelled to leave the chamber if he is not going to vote. I am against compulsion, and if it were necessary to do so I would be prepared to move an amendment to the new standing order as proposed by the special committee. I am hoping that the matter will be put up to the committee and a standing vote taken, either for or against it, but I did want to register my protest.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had
intended to make some extended observations with respect to the general aspects of the report of this committee, but since much of the ground, has been covered by those who have spoken I shall confine myself to three or four matters which I think are germane to the subject under discussion. In his first speech in connection with this matter His Honour the Speaker referred to the fact that no suggestions had been offered in writing to the committee by members of the house, nor had they accepted the invitation sent out by the committee to present suggestions as to the changing of the rules, i think many hon. members feel as I do, that if a formal invitation to present verbal suggestions to the committee had been given it would have been more acceptable. I believe that would have brought forth many suggestions. I only say this because His Honour the Speaker made some mention of it. It is one thing to put suggestions in writing and quite another thing, and I am sure much more valuable, to go to a committee and give suggestions or evidence as may be required.
One matter that has been dealt with very lightly is the question of reading speeches in the house. I do not intend to dwell too much on this because I am free to admit that I would rather hear read a well prepared speech than I would to listen to a poorly delivered speech, even though it may actually be a better one. There is sometimes an advantage in having remarks put in a condensed form and read. However, my remarks must
Rules of the House

not be taken as an endorsation of the reading of speeches in this house. Frankly I think it ought to be discouraged. Debate in the House of Commons is of most use to the people and to the house when it comes freely from the representatives of the people.
I remember one experienced parliamentarian who is no longer in the house but who continues to follow the debates very carefully and studiously. He told me that he never reads the debates which occur while Mr. Speaker is in the chair because he never knew from reading Hansard whether they had been read, whether they had been prepared by the member himself or whether they represented a thesis or some philosophical utterance which was being placed upon Hansard. He read only what occurred in the committee stage of a bill or a resolution. It seemed to him that that is when the best debate occurs. If I may say so, it is at that time that we hear from hon. members what they would be likely to say in normal conversation. I have listened to some experienced debaters, and I notice that except on rare occasions when a statement has to be letter perfect they do not read their speeches. We offer a poor example to have speeches read in the house, and it should be avoided if possible. However, like everything else I do not suppose any hard-and-fast rule can be followed and I repeat the reservation which I made at the beginning of my remarks.
There is one more matter I should like to bring to the attention of the committee. I think most hon. members have come to the conclusion that there is something wrong in the division of a private member's time. The average elector fails to realize the amount of work a conscientious, industrious and hardworking private member of parliament has to do. I have been a private member myself, and I still am classed in that category. I have found, and I think most private members have found, that the mornings are largely taken up with correspondence, interviews and taking care of various odds and ends. This constitutes one of the most tedious and perhaps hardest tasks a member has to do. If an hon. member takes an active part in committees, he must attend committee meetings during the mornings and perhaps in the afternoons as well. Then he has the afternoon and evening sessions of the house to attend.
I should like to make a suggestion, although I am not sure that it can be properly accepted. However, unless we have suggestions we shall not be able to arrive at definite conclusions. When the days of war stress have passed, when the cabinet and the government have more time at their disposal to devote to

ordinary matters, the time of a private member should be worked out on a different basis. I hasten to point out that this is not a wartime recommendation; it is one for the more normal and perhaps more leisurely days which we hope will come with peace. I think the private member ought to have his mornings free from parliamentary duties in this chamber or in committee. The afternoon sittings of the house might perhaps begin at an earlier hour and extend a little later than six o'clock. Perhaps a six-hour sitting could be arranged without much dislocation by starting a little earlier and ending later in the afternoon, leaving the evenings free for private members to do their committee work. That might establish a better balance for the ordinary private member of the house, because there is no doubt that the average private member, if he is a busy member, has an overlapping and duplication of his duties from time to time from which he should have some relief so far as the rules of the house will permit. I hasten to point out again that I am not proposing this as a solution of the problem but simply throwing out the suggestion in the hope that its advantages and disadvantages might be considered.
It is difficult to arbitrarily restrict members of the house in their speaking time, but from my own brief experience in the house, while I have perhaps never made any very effective speeches in the house, as most hon. members will agree, I do say, open confession being good for the soul, that the most effective speech I have ever delivered in the house as a private member, if this may be used as a yardstick at all, is one that I made on a budget debate when I spoke for' only two and a half minutes. At all events I am proudest of that speech as I stand here to-night.
It is all very well to say that parliament must be shorn of much of its debating rights, but we must use caution in this matter because the interests of the constituencies which private members represent must be safeguarded, and when their interests are at stake there should not, of course, be any undue curtailment of speeches by their representatives. Parliament is often spoken of as being the safety-valve of the nation. While I object to long speeches and to repetition, and I think we all must share guilt in that respect, let us not forget that it is better for discussion to take place in the House of Commons than in the cellars of the nation, for where there is a damming up of free expression, there is no safety-valve and an explosion may take place. That is a matter which may properly be of concern to the house.

Rules oj the House
There is a germ of assistance in the suggestion that has been advanced that there should be a better organization of our debates which would assist in forming a more favourable public opinion, and public opinion, of course, is of great consequence to this chamber at all times. It is important that we should keep the prestige of this chamber as high as possible, also our standards of debate. There have been times, I believe, when the public feels that this chamber has taken too much time in debating subjects which have not seemingly been, of as great interest to the public at large.
Another great difficulty, so far as the public is concerned, is that during the war so much legislation has been taken out of the hands of the legislative chamber and passed through administrative orders and orders in council. That has been dealt with before, and I have no desire to enlarge upon it to-night except to say that since the War Measures Act was put into operation there have been many times and are times and perhaps will be times again when the government has mistaken the urgency of the situation and resorted to that method of legislating, as witness the 42,000 orders in council passed by this government. I want to protest against that method except in cases where the emergency is of the urgent character contemplated by the War Measures Act itself.	#
Coming to the proposed amendment to standing order 9, I find myself very much in agreement with the opinions expressed to-night by the hon. member for New Westminster. It seems to me that we should not compel a member to cast his vote in a division in this house. There are two reasons for that which will at once occur to [DOT] every hon. member. I am not going to go into the pros and cons of compulsory voting throughout the country, but so long as we have not yet adopted compulsory voting for the electors, and so long as we do not compel a voter, once he gets into the polling booth, to cast his vote for any particular candidate-he may spoil his ballot or not mark it at all-we have no right to apply a different set of rules to the representatives of those electors in this House of Commons. I just say that by way of emphasizing the argument so well advanced by the hon. member for New Westminster to-night. I take my stand against compelling members to vote in this house.
The procedure of the house in dealing with estimates is dealt with in the general introduction to the committee's report, and I am in agreement with what it says as to estimates. I think it would tend to get away from ministerial responsibility to take consideration of
the estimates away from the committee of the whole and assign that work to a smaller committee. It may be argued that it would save time, but I am doubtful of that. It might even increase the time which would be taken up in debate in this house. I do not think the suggestion is feasible and I suggest that the committee was right in opposing it. I have dealt with these matters briefly because there are a number of other matters which will have to be discussed as we reach the various proposed amendments to standing orders. Anything further I have to say I shall defer until the other amendments are before us.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I am at a loss to know whether I am out in the wilderness. I do not know whether I shall be in order in making a few remarks with regard to the principles of this report; but my understanding was that the amendment to standing order 9 has been introduced and that a free discussion may be had on that amendment.
As a member of the special committee, and, may I say, having had some experience in serving on committees, I never knew of a committee where there was such unified intent on the part of the members to carry out the purpose for which it was constituted. I firmly believe that, but for our persistent adherence to the principle which we believed we were required to follow, that of expediting the work of the house and at the same time preserving the rights of minority groups, more recommendations would have appeared in the report. Yet I believe, in spite of restrictions on that account, the committee has made recommendations which will expedite the work of this house, and that no minority group will suffer thereby.
While we were unanimous on the principle of the recommendations which we submitted, there were some differences with regard to certain of the items. I do not mind confessing that when the matter of curtailing the time for speeches was before the committee, I advocated that instead of forty minutes being the duration of the time for speech making, it be reduced to thirty minutes. Possibly I was not alone in this respect. I advanced this change on account of an opinion which I hold in this regard that, apart from ministers of the crown or others who possibly would not be reckoned as back-benchers, we can say in thirty minutes all the worth-while things on any subject. I have been a listener-in so often, in this chamber and out of it, to men who made excellent speeches so long as they stopped at thirty minutes, but spent ten more minutes-[DOT]

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
In listening to the able speeches which have been delivered by hon. members, I have noticed a contradiction in the speech of the leader of the opposition. He said in the first place that the free expression of views in this chamber was a safety-valve, but afterwards he spoke of wasted time. This is contradictory. He may feel that the speech of a fellow member is a waste of time, and have a different opinion about his own. That is human; I do not blame him for that. The retort which comes from any hon. member when one asks the specific question, "What is wasted time?" is, "Your own speeches". Then everybody will laugh, and there will be an end of it; it will be regarded as a conclusive retort by many parliamentarians to the fellow who is caught in that trap because he spoke too much. It is a very easy answer: "Did you do it?" "No, I did not do it; you are the one that did it." Laughter, cheers, applause. Most conclusive, very weighty. But one should be more specific than that. The leader of the opposition must say what he means by "wasted time". He was the first who spoke about it; whenever he speaks, or one of his party speaks, that is not wasted time_, but time usefully spent for the good of the nation; but if another hon. member disagrees with them, he speaks too much; he is wasting time and his speeches cost so much to the Canadian poeple. That is the first point.
[Mr. McGarry.l
The second thing I noticed in his short speech is what he said in pressing the adoption of the amendments to the rules of the house. He rose very often to insist upon the Prime Minister so amending the rules that there should be no waste of time, and what does he propose to us? He proposes a brain diet for parliament after the war. It is a post-war programme which he gives us. In the morning, no sittings of parliament, no sittings of committees; in the afternoon, another little diet; at night, another little diet. Three diets, one for correspondence, one for committees, one for sittings of the house, and it will be for appreciation after the war. It is not necessary now, and if it is not necessary now let us drop it, finish it and * take up something else. If the hon. gentleman does not hold the view that it is important to amend at this time the rules of the house, let us finish it right now by dropping it in the waste-paper basket, the place where it belongs. It is the kind of thing which the Canadian people should not have to listen to. Speaking here on behalf even of members of the Tory party who do not recognize the importance of the matter and do not realize that when the election comes there will be hecklers in their own counties who will ask them to report on what has been done by their leaders themselves about this most important question, the defence of parliamentary liberties, T would ask them, what will they have to answer? Poison is given them by speeches like that of the leader of the opposition. He has depreciated the work of parliament; he has spoken of wasted time.
I remember wasted time when Arthur Meighen was leader of the opposition; wasted time- lots of it-when Bennett the humbug was Prime Minister of Canada; wasted time when all the other gentlemen whom I have known, so many of those who have led the Tory party, one after the other, in the house, wasted time; when the hon. member for York-Sunbury was making speeches which lasted for hours; when there was a marathon of speeches all the time between the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition. And if it was wasted time for the Prime Minister to speak for hours, it was even more a waste of time for the then leader of the opposition to speak for hours.
The present leader of the opposition tells us that on one occasion he spoke for two and a half minutes and that he did not waste time. Well, wasting time is a relative matter. One could waste time speaking for one minute, and even half a minute might be a waste of time. It would be a waste of time on the part of the present leader of the opposition, because

Rules of the House
the best speech he could make would be a wink-say it with flowers. The hon. gentleman is a most likable man. In fact, he is the first one I have seen in that seat, in the twenty years that I have been a member of parliament, who could be said to be a likable man. That is why he has not been chosen leader of his party. That is the reason. The reason is an obvious one; they always choose the wrong man. They did so the last time, and when they select a leader they have the next one in mind. They are untruthful when they select the leader of the party.
I am discussing w'hat the hon. member has referred to as waste of time, and when we come to this very important matter I want hon. members to realize exactly how important it is. I was greatly offended and shocked when I heard the hon. gentleman say, "We will come to more important matters afterwards." It may be more important to him to discuss trivial matters such as garbage and recuperation, but he must know that there are spiritual values and certain rights that count for much more than an ash-can even if it is kept in a million-dollar building. That is why I call the attention of the members of the opposition to the importance of spiritual values which are a legacy to us from our forefathers and which were worth fighting for, and it is for that reason that to-day I protest most energetically and emphatically against the first three pages of this pronunciamento, in which every sentence swears at the sentence following. It is something most incredible. It is not hash; it is not a stew; it is what we call in French gachis-something incredible, an incredible mess. We are to stand for it because it is supposed to be the basis of the amendments that appear on that paper.
I do not believe that members of parliament will support it. It is beyond my expectation. I might have expected the worst, but I did not expect this. It is worse than the worst. Those who will come after us, whether we are successful or not; those who have been opposing this matter from the start, the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill), the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy), and some others who have opposed it on basic grounds, will deserve the gratitude of future members of parliament.
Not long ago the Prime Minister said something that gives us food for thought. It is food for thought for many members of parliament. He said that after the next election there will be great changes in the House of Commons. Did he mean by that that the members who were supporting these amendments were putting a rope round their necks? I do not know, but I presume the Prime Minister is clever enough to have meant that when
he made that statement in this chamber. I do not see, therefore, why we should have to carry the burden of these contradictory and unacceptable statements, like the Volga boatman, during the whole term of our parliamentary life.
It is time to get down to brass tacks and to realize that when a member makes a speech that is not satisfactory to some other member he exercises the right that is his and the right which that other himself can exercise at any time, and therefore what is being said by a handful of members, who, I hope, represent the opinion of the majority of their colleagues, is that these three pages should be censored by the committee, that they should disappear from the official publication, and the other amendments be considered in turn. In my view, the thing has to be done for the safeguarding of our parliamentary institutions, for the safeguarding of our liberties, and when during the next elections, whenever they come, anyone who has supported official statements of this kind, when addressing the people, need not be surprised if he or she is heckled. Such persons will get only what they deserve because, if our rights are not safeguarded, if the charter of our parliamentary liberties is changed, they will have no reason to complain should they encounter any trouble in addressing audiences outside parliament.
This is my last appeal. I hope that the committee will consider the matter carefully; Someone says, "Oh, oh". That hon. member who says "oh, oh," will be defeated by a huge majority at the next election. He had better look around him at the lights in the chamber; he had better look at the carving of the moose around the ladies' gallery, because it will be the last time he will see these sights, and I will give him a picture of the House of Commons to put in his living-room so that he may remember the days when he was a member of parliament and when he said "oh, oh", when. I was discussing a serious matter.

speechtext:
Before dealing with the immediate amendment to the standing order in question I want to take the privilege granted by the leader of the house, and taken advantage of by several members of the committee, in order to consider for a moment that portion of the report which has been variously described as a running commentary, a prelude, an introduction and by several othe. names, but never really identified in all its nakedness. I wish to mention one or two things, but I do not want to be charged with holding up the committee. There are two points I should like to bring to the atte ntion of the committee in this regard, and i ne if
Rules oj the House

in connection with the reading of speeches, a question touched on by the leader of the opposition. If this house really wants to expedite its business it should have put that proposal at the very top of the list as an instruction, that there should be no speeches read in this House of Commons. The reading of speeches is the cause of more delay than anything else, but personally I share the view of the leader of the opposition; I would rather listen to a well read speech than a badly delivered one. Because a man reads his speech it does not follow that it has been prepared by some sinister hand outside the house; not at all. There are very able men who can express themselves well in writing, if given time, but who cannot do so spontaneously, and who cannot learn their speeches by heart. Personally I would be in favour of letting them read their speeches, but for one thing; that is, I always object to lending myself to the doing of anything that is made into a farce, and this prohibition against the reading of speeches in this house is absolutely a farce. No genuine attempt is made to enforce it. I am not saying anything against the present Speaker or the present Chairman; I have been here for many years, and it was always the same. The Speaker hesitates to call a man to order, and if he does so the man simply says, "No, Mr. Speaker, I am only adhering somewhat closely to my notes."

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Then why not let him hand in the speech to Hansard without reading it?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Some men, of course, have good eyesight and can do what I cannot; that is, read their speeches at a distance. I have only notes, and I must look at them closely, but I have seen men give the impression that they were delivering a speech with the aid of but very few notes, while actually they were reading every word of it. Quite inadvertently the other evening I happened to pass behind one of these hon. gentlemen; I looked down at his desk and saw that he had the whole thing written out, even to commas, semicolons, subheads and so on. While listening to him I had the impression that he was not reading his speech, because he did not need to look at it too often, but actually he was reading every word. So that if we are really sincere in wanting to save the time of the house, let us enforce that rule. No one is trying to enforce it now, but if the rule is retained it should be enforced.
I wished to refer to one other matter which should engage the attention of this house and which should have been dealt with by the special committee, which steered clear of it

entirely. That is, they should have brought in, and we should pass here to-night, an amendment providing that the defeat of the government on a petty matter shall not mean its resignation. An adverse vote on a small amendment to some bill, for instance, should not be regarded as a defeat of the government. While perhaps comparatively few hon. members would admit it, I am sure that on many occasions they would have voted differently if it had not been for that custom. A loyal supporter of a party does not like to vote against it; when the whip comes along and tells him that the government will have to resign if they are defeated on some small matter, which will mean an election, he says, "WTell, boys, I did not like that bill but I could not face an election just now." Because of appeals to his loyalty to his party many a man must vote in a way he would never dream of voting if it were left to his own conscience. Why should that be the case? It was never so in the old days. I recall that in the legislature at Victoria a party came in with a very slim majority; if one member went out to have a drink or to get his hair cut, the government might be defeated before he came back. The government, very sensibly, said, "We are going back to the custom of fifty years ago; we are not going to regard an adverse vote in this house as a vote of want of confidence unless it is on a resolution which contains those precise words." That is the proper way to do it. Let the opposition, if they feel strong enough, move that the house no longer has confidence in the government; that is the way to defeat it. Many years ago, when I was quite a young man, it was the custom in Britain-I do not know what it was here-that a government would never resign because they were defeated in the country. They always met the house, even though they knew they were hopelessly in the minority. Then the leader of the opposition would rise and make a motion of want of confidence; it would pass, the government would be formally and officially defeated and would resign.
Now the custom has grown up, though not supported by any rule of law so far as I know, that when a government is defeated at an election it packs its bags and steps out. Whether or not that custom should be adhered to is not so important; the important thing is that no hon. member should be compelled by a sense of loyalty or for any other reason to vote against his own conscience, because it might mean the defeat of the government. There is no reason why a provision such as I have suggested should not be adopted. I am quite certain it would make for better government, because I have seen things pass in this house that never would have passed if they

Rules oj the House
had been left to open votes. I do not know why on earth the committee did not deal with this most important question.
I now come back to the amendment we are supposed to be discussing; that is, the amendment which proposes to compel every hon. member who is in his place to vote, whether or not he knows what he is voting about. The hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie made a point this evening with which I had not dealt. He said that the alternative to voting would be for a man to go outside the chamber before the vote took place. I could not hear the hon. member very clearly, but I take it he was referring to an instance which occurred only a few weeks ago, when we took votes on several amendments to the main motion. One vote was taken, then another, and finally the last vote was taken without ringing the bell at all, and without giving anyone outside an opportunity to come in. In that instance a rank injustice might have been perpetrated. A few months ago I sat here during a division and did not vote. To tell the truth I have forgotten what was the occasion, but I was quite decided that neither party had a good case, and I did not see why I should express sympathy with either side. I felt they were both playing politics and that there was no need for me te endorse the one side or the other.
What was the purpose in mind in setting up this committee? It was "to simplify, accelerate and expedite the business of the house." I do not know why it was necessary to put in the two words; either "expedite" or "accelerate" would have been sufficient, but that was what the committee was appointed for; that was what we call the reference, what we told them to do. How are we to expedite the business of the house by adopting this amendment? We have been told that this is an urgent matter, that the public demand it, but that is all bunk. No one is demanding it; no one is outspoken about, it. It is some thirteen years since this matter has been brought up, and there has never been any trouble about it. Not since 1906, which is thirty-eight years ago, hap the British parliament, to which we look for guidance in cases of this kind, forced anyone to vote whether or not he wanted to do so. Surely, as some hon. members have said, we can leave it to the honour of a member, and to his constituents. The constituents do keep note of how their members vote, and they would be quick to ask, " Why didn't you vote this way or the other?"
Then a man might have private reasons for not voting. I believe there is a rule of the house, though I have not had time to look it up, which says that a man may not vote if his 100-149
private, pecuniary interests are involved. For instance, he should not vote on a bill to give a franchise to some company in which he had a financial interest. The house does not always know a man's private affairs. He might have a perfectly proper pecuniary interest in a company and his sense of honour would lead him to abstain from voting. Then fie would be compelled to stand up and be pilloried. He would be asked, "Why did you not vote?" He would reply, " I had my own reasons for not voting." Then he might be told that was not sufficient, after which the absurd procedure of naming the hon. member would be gone through, though that died out a hundred years ago, and ostensibly he would be committed to the tower. I remember that on one occasion a man was committed to the tower in Victoria, which meant the best hotel in town. By and by the government realized what idiots they were making of themselves and said to the man, "You can come out." He replied, " Not if I know it. I am living comfortably here; I can come and go as I please all day," and he stayed there until the end of the session, when the law automatically let him out. It is a very unpleasant experience, as some of us here know, to be named. It is a disgrace. It is put on the record, and it stands against a man for all time-that he has been named, and escorted by a policeman outside of the chamber.
It is not necessary to do that, unless it is absolutely unavoidable. A question of religion might be involved. I might say to some of my people, "I am not in favour of that, but I will tell you what I will do; I will do nothing against it; I will not vote against it if it comes up." Here, in one way or another, I am obliged to do something against my promise and my conscience.
Can anyone tell us where there is any precedent for such a rule? Great Britain has gone on for thirty-eight years, and we have gone on for a number of years without enforcing it. Who asked for it? I ask this: Will that simplify, accelerate or expedite the business of the house? Every time this comes up there will be a squabble about it, and someone will put up a fight. If a person must give his reasons he is perhaps revealing his private affairs. Will that expedite the business of the house? I can remember Miss Macphail being compelled to vote. There was a complaint about it, and it led to our adopting a rule, more or less unwritten, that we should never compel anyone to vote.
The penalty is so severe that it is undesirable. I submit that the proposed amendment ought to be thrown out, because it is contrary to the instructions we gave the committee.

Rules of the House

We instructed that committee to take steps to accelerate the business of the house. I can safely say that that will not accelerate the business of the house.
I am glad to see how many are willing to vote against this change. And having had all this discussion, I find, as a matter of fact, that that is the rule now. The present penalty is not put in, but the only difference is the penalty. It is a very unjust penalty. Let me refer the committee to citation 68, standing order 9:
If a member who has heard the question put does not vote, and the attention of the Speaker is directed to the fact, the latter will call upon him to declare on which side he votes; and his name will be recorded accordingly.
But, following the custom, and by agreement on both sides of the house, that was abandoned. Its abandonment was animated by common sense, and it was dropped out. Why is there all this fuss about putting it in now, with this very unjust and unfair penalty?
The hon. member for New Westminster has said something about moving an amendment. He does not need to do so. All he needs to do is vote against this abortion of a rule.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have no desire to get into this discussion. However, if someone did not take part it would continue as a two-man show. I am surprised at this debate. A House of Commons committee was appointed for the purpose of bringing in recommendations as to how the work of the house might best be carried out. In my opinion it requires and can stand considerable improvement. Each group in the house was privileged to appoint members to the committee, and the committee sat under the chairmanship of Mr. Speaker, a man whom we all respect, whose fairness we recognize and in whose judgment we have confidence.
Under his chairmanship the committee, as is set out in the preamble to the report, asked any hon. members who so desired to place their views on procedure before the committee in writing. As the preamble states, no suggestions were received. If we were interested in expediting the business of the house, in protecting the interests of private members, and in all those other things we now appear to fear, then certainly we were lax in our duty in not assisting the committee to come to an understanding in accordance with our views. No member of the house availed himself of the invitation by the committee to send it the benefit of our views.
One would have to listen carefully to realize that we are discussing standing order 9, and the preamble to the report. Any committee which understood its business would,

in dealing with a matter of this kind, write a preamble to any specific recommendations it might have to offer. So far as I am concerned, I believe this matter was considered carefully by the committee, while a member of this group was listening in. We have confidence in the man we placed on that committee. Reading the preamble to the report, I must say I can find nothing wrong with it.
For example, it states that one day of each week should be set aside for the purpose of discussing supply. Surely that is an improvement on sneaking into supply at ten minutes to eleven at night. No one knows when we are going to have supply, and all are guessing about it. The committee, in the preamble, definitely suggests that we set aside one day a week for that purpose; and with that suggestion I find no fault.
They set out the many problems with which they had to contend, and they have expressed the fear of interfering with the rights and privileges of anyone. They point out the difficulties .connected with amending regulations or standing orders, particularly in view of the war situation, and the encroachment the government has already made on the privileges of private members.
Then they suggest that where a protracted debate is likely to take place, in order to give each member an opportunity to express the views of his particular group, representatives of each group should meet. That is a matter of custom; it is done anyway. It is merely a reiteration of a custom which has grown up in the past. So far as I can see, there is nothing wrong with the preamble.
I am not going to say anything about the other specific recommendations. I have, however, this to say about standing order 9, which we are now discussing. A member of the House of Commons is sent here to represent his constituency. What he does in the house is not his business; rather it is the business of the people who sent him here. He will have an opinion on any legislation passing through the house. Such legislation will be either good or bad for his constituents. They are not able to judge, but he is. He sits here, listens, takes part in the debate and has an understanding of the legislation. If he is in his seat in the chamber, it is his obligation to vote, and it is his responsibility to his constituents to show them, by the written record of the house, how he voted, whether he was taking care of their interests, or otherwise. If he wishes to leave the chamber and say he vras not present, that is his own responsibility.
But I believe it should be the duty of members of the House of Commons to vote,

Rules of the House
and it should be the duty of those enforcing the rules to see to it that when the bell rings the members are in their seats. When a motion or an amendment is before the house, one which means something to a member's constituents, it is his moral obligation to show them how he voted on that motion, and to show whether or not he was interested in their welfare. I do not think there should be any argument about that. For any hon. member to take the position that what he does is his own business alone is not my conception of carrying out the duty devolving upon a member of parliament. I consider myself to be the spokesman of the people of my constituency and of the people of the Dominion of Canada. The people of my constituency have sent me here with certain hopes and aspirations as to the manner in which I will carry out my responsibilities in taking care of their problems. What I do in this house should be done with a thought to the welfare of my constituents. Any matter that is before this house offers me a supreme test as to whether or not I am interested in it, whether or not I have the courage of my convictions. I must consider what action I shall take, whether it is good or bad for me politically. I do not think any member who is in his seat when a vote is taken should shirk his duty to his constituents.
I am surprised at the length of time that has been spent in discussing this matter. I think the committee have done as good a job as they could in the time at their disposal, having regard to the many complications surrounding the matter. I consider that the amendment to standing order 9 is quite good and should be accepted, plus the preamble. We will speak about the other amendments as we come to them.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I am glad to learn from the previous speaker that we are discussing an amendment and the preamble, since I have been trying to find out about that. This afternoon I listened to some long speeches in connection with the suggestions contained in the preamble. I must confess that I am not entirely in sympathy with those who object to them. I see no harm in those recommendations, but at the same time I would not care to cast my vote for all that is expressed in the prologue. I do not agree with the contention expressed in the second paragraph. I shall not take the time to read it; I simply make that statement. I do not agree with the statement made in the first part of the third paragraph, which reads:
The present procedure was devised to reflect the freedom of all the members of the house, but we must realize that in war time parliament 100-149J
is bound to divest itself of some of its prerogatives in order to strengthen the government's power.
I absolutely do not believe that statement; I absolutely am not in favour of that statement. My contention is that the government has too much power, that it has taken unto itself more power than parliament ever intended it should have. I quite agree that parliament should give way to war-time legislation, but for my part I will not let it go by without vigorous protest. I do not agree to giving the government more power. The fact of the matter is that power in a demorcracy rests with the people, not with the government. In Canada parliament is the body which represents the people; the government does not represent the people. The government is the administrative body that has been called upon to execute the legislation that parliament puts into effect. But the government does not represent the people; parliament represents the people.
I should like to say a word with regard to the amendment to standing order 9. I cannot say that I have any objection to this amendment. I do not agree with some who have contended that a man should not be in his seat in the chamber when a vote is taken if he is not going to vote. I do not know why he needs to be here if he is not going to vote, unless it be to watch the rest of us perform as we make our little bows to His Honour. When a standing vote is taken the bells are rung for two or three minutes, and if an hon. member does not want to vote he has plenty of time to go to the lobby, put his feet up on a chair and smoke his pipe if he wants to while the rest of us decide which way we intend to vote.
If this amendment carries I fancy it will put an end to the custom of pairing. I do not know why pairing is allowed. Personally I never could see any wisdom in that practice. I think it tends to encourage loyalty to party rather than loyalty to the people. When a man must be away he gets a member on the other side to refrain from voting in order that the parties may still retain their proper standing. I do not go much for party machinery. I think private members when they take their places in the house should do so as representing the people, rather than a party. Having made these observations, I am prepared to favour the ameudment to standing order 9.
