speechtext:
The committee is discussing the report of the special committee appointed to revise the standing orders of the
Rules of the House

House of Commons. I desire to renew my plea for greater independence on the part of private members. I set this forth in a speech I made on February 8, which is reported on page 263 of Hansard as follows:
To this end members of parliament, especially in this time of world crisis, ought to exercise their right to advocate and consider legislation with less regard to party affiliation. Members now have freedom, in theory but not ip general practice, of voting according to their judgment. Consequently I advocate that the defeat of a government measure shall not constitute defeat of the government.
Confidence or want of confidence in the government, after non-acceptance of proposed legislation, should ibe determined by a separate vote. An adverse majority on a confidence vote would then constitute defeat of the government.
In the United States there is no such thing as a vote adverse to the administration. An adverse vote means no more than a favourable vote. Under their constitution an election is held every four years, and consequently members of the senate or the house of representatives need not fear that they are forcing a defeat of the government and bringing on a general election when they vote in a certain way.
Since I offered those suggestions on February 8 I have had much favourable comment in editorials and in very kind letters sent to me by Canadians from all parts of the country. I have some evidence that in emergencies this practice of continuing in office even in the face of an adverse vote is being employed. For instance, I find an article in the Toronto Globe and Mail of February 25, which carries the following heading: "Premier Drew prepared to accept test on confidence." Premier Drew's comments at that time were as follows:
This is not a minority government. It is the government called to give executive direction to the affairs of this legislature. It may be a healthy thing to see members free to express their own opinions and vote in accordance with their own views.
This cannot be a minority government. You have the power to move a want-of-confidence motion which we will ibe glad to accept as an issue. If this is not done, we must imply you have confidence in the continuance of our work as the government of the province.
As for the terms on which we will govern, there are no terms and no thought of dictatorship. Even a hint of dictatorship is a reflection on the man who makes it.
We are in the position where we must depend entirely on your support of what is done.
We do not intend to govern in a spirit of fear. We assume full responsibility, and as soon as you feel we have not confidence, the democratic test is there.
We have another instance of a government arriving at a situation in which they had difficulty. I have in my hand a Canadian Press

dispatch dated March 28, from London, and it is headed: "No censure intended in vote against government." Members will recall that on that day Prime Minister Churchill's government suffered the first defeat in its history by a single vote. The situation was reviewed, and on the following day, on a definite vote of confidence or no confidence, the government was sustained by an overwhelming majority.
What is the effect in parliament of the practice that the government is defeated on an adverse vote? One serious drawback is that private members supporting a government that has a very large majority need give no concern to studying the legislation that is before parliament. If they take their cue from the Prime Minister or the cabinet ministers as to how they will vote what need it matter whether they give any study whatever to the legislation or not? I can say to any young man in Canada who is contemplating entry into parliament that he will be grateful if when he comes into this house he finds himself on the opposition benches because there he has an opportunity to speak whenever he wishes, whereas on the other side of the house, according to the practice that prevails of ministers leading and carrying on the discussions, there is very little for private members supporting the government to do when that government has a large majority. Therefore I would say that in the interests of careful consideration of legislation, members, if they will not do it of their own accord, should be forced into the position where they must study the legislation in order that they may know how they should cast their vote when the division bell rings. I do not desire to enlarge on this point, but I think Mr. Speaker and his committee would do well to consider, if possible at this time, a further amendment to the standing orders in order that private members may be given additional freedom and additional encouragement to take a greater interest in the legislation that is presented day by day. I am sure that the effect of forcing private members into the position where they must study the legislation in order to know how to vote would go a long way toward keeping this chamber filled during the discussions and get us out of the present situation in which we are criticized for taking little or no interest in what is going on.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wonder if I may say one word in regard to the exact issue as between the proposed amendment and the present state of the rules. If hon. members will look

Rules of the House
at citation 69, on standing order 9, in Beau-chesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, second edition, page 25, they will see that the last part of that paragraph reads:
The practice has not been changed in Canada where every member who has heard the question put is bound to vote.
The citation in that book has not the force or sanction of a standing order, and the amendment proposed by the special committee to the house would make it a rule as part' of standing order 9. If the proposed amendment is defeated, the practice of the house, according to its custom, will be exactly what it is now, but His Honour the Speaker will not have a definite rule with the sanction of a standing order to guide him in ruling when occasions arise as they did between 1930 and 1935, as those of us who were in the house then will recall, when there was uncertainty because the practice was not embodied in a standing order. That is the issue concisely and clearly. Whether the amendment is defeated or not we will still have the practice, but the Speaker will not have a definite standing order to guide him in the decisions he has to make.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Can the hon. member find the same wording that he quoted in the third edition of Beauchesne? I presume, if we are to be guided at all, we are to be guided by the latest edition of Beauchesne, and I am unable to find that wording in the third edition.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I was unable to find it repeated in the third edition, may I inform my hon. friend. It is only a comment of the clerk of the house and has not the force or sanction of a standing order. Any observer can make such comments as he sees fit, but they are not binding on the house. The citation quoted only indicates what the practice of this house has been, and the practice has been in force as a matter of custom, but not as a matter of law and not because of a standing order.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
As to the observations made by the Minister of Pensions and National Health, I think I am bound to take issue with him. His argument is based on a citation on the standing orders in the book prepared by Doctor Beauchesne on the rules of the house. These marginal notes are only an indication or a recording of the practice of the house; they are a record of decisions of Speakers in the Chair, but there is no rule of the house and no standing order existent at the present moment obliging a member to register his vote. There is nothing beyond a citation which has been written out of the precedents which
have prevailed in the past. But I have observed that for a number of years, five or even ten years, the practice has changed, and hon. members have been allowed to remain in their seats and not register their votes on the question. Thus a new practice has been developed which contradicts to a certain extent the marginal note referred to by the minister. At present hon. members are at liberty, according to a practice which has prevailed for several years, not to vote on a question when they feel they are not bound to do so, or when they are not convinced that it is proper or in the interests of their constituents to vote yes or no. This may happen very often on a matter of relative unimportance, upon questions which are coloured by political advantage for one party or the other. An hon. member may feel that he should not take side on an issue which is purely political and which has no other purpose than to reap some political advantage later on.
I am in favour of every member of the house being at liberty to register his vote or to refrain from registering it. The argument has been advanced that we are speaking here for our electors. It is true that each of us represents a section of the country, but it is left to the member to execute his mandate according to his own judgment. If he feels that there is no justification for his registering a vote on a question of no importance, or when, in his judgment, a case has not been made out, he should be free to refrain from doing so, and if there is any criticism to be made of his action, let the electors who sent him here make that criticism. It is not for the house; it is not, with all due respect, for the Speaker, and it is not for the government to impose upon a member an obligation to vote when according to his conscience and his judgment he feels he should not register a vote. Liberty should be preserved to the member to decide that matter for himself.
I do not like the severity of the amendment which is proposed. It seems to me that the penalty to be imposed is much too severe and too great for the offence. It is though we ' were to decide that a man should be hanged because he stole a bottle of whisky. The penalty is out of proportion to the offence.
I propose to vote against the amendment. It is not on account of any fear I entertain of expressing my opinion on any question which is brought before the house, or that I am afraid of expressing my views on any matter which is being discussed in public or in this chamber. I am going to* vote against it because it changes a practice which has prevailed for several years, and because I want to preserve the liberty of a member to decide what he is going
Rules oj the House

to do in this house and in what way he will represent the electors who have sent him here.
So much for the amendment. But it has not been made clear to me exactly what proposal we are discussing or arguing. The whole afternoon we have heard arguments against the preamble to these proposed amendments, and a very strong case has been made against the suggestions contained in the preamble. What is at present before the committee? It is a report of a special committee appointed apparently to improve the business, the deliberations of the House of Commons. That report is composed of two sections. In the first section will be found recommendations or suggestions or advices which are being given, without stating that they should be embodied in any standing order, but nevertheless suggestions which are of a very important and serious character and which, if applied, might raise sound objections and are likely to curtail the discussion in this House of Commons to a dangerous degree and prevent groups and minorities from expressing their views with regard to questions which come up for discussion here. We are told that these are only pious wishes, that they are merely suggestions; but that is a point of view expressed by those who have delivered speeches supporting the report. We have a document which has been placed before us in accordance with a motion by the Prime Minister. He moved:
That Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of the whole to consider the report of the special committee on the revision of standing orders.
And the question being put on the said motion it was agreed to. The house accordingly resolved itself into committee of the whole on the said report, and progress having been made and reported, the committee obtained leave to consider it again at the next sitting of the house.
We are at present considering the report of the special committee appointed to revise the standing orders; and when all the amendments proposed are approved, or some of them disapproved, and you, Mr. Chariman, make your report to Mr. Speaker, you will report that the committee of the whole has been considering the report of the special committee. So that if we agree to the report made to Mr. Speaker, approving the report of the special committee, it will mean that the, House of Commons has also approved the recommendations or the suggestions or advices included in the preamble of that report. You cannot separate the two things. If we do not

agree about the preamble, let us advise the Chairman not to report on the report of the special committee but only on the amendments which have been considered by the committee of the whole, if such a procedure is permissible.
I think we should have some clarification of the situation so that we may know exactly what we are dealing with. Are we dealing solely with the amendments proposed, or are we dealing indirectly with the suggestions or proposals contained in the preamble of the report? This ought to be made clear. The report is rather awkward because it contains two sections which do not agree. If what is contained in the preamble is worth our consideration, why did the committee not suggest some amendments to carry out the proposals contained in the preamble? It is an indirect way of amending the rules or suggesting a method of procedure to the government with regard to the transacting of the business of the house.
I am inclined to agree that it would not be necessary to have the suggestions contained in the preamble clearly embodied as standing orders, because practically all the suggestions that are made in the preamble can be put into effect as the rules stand at present. They are suggestions that are made to the government as to procedure. But if we approve the report as it is before us at present, we approve the suggestions that the special committee has been making to the government, and we authorize the government to proceed according to these suggestions. And possibly not this government, but some other government might look upon it as a precedent and might say, if the same questions should arise later on, "Well, the procedure that we are at present following has been suggested to us by a special committee appointed to consider the standing orders, and the suggested methods of directing the debates of the House of Commons have been approved by the whole House of Commons, so that we are justified in following those suggestions now, since they constitute a precedent approved by members of the House of Commons sitting as committee of the whole."
That is why I insist upon some clarification being made of the situation and some clear indication being given to us as to what we are really voting on at the present time. I would be inclined to accept the statement that has been made, if I remember correctly, by the Minister of National Defence, that the preamble contains only the pious wishes and advice and recommendations of the committee, which the government is not bound to follow or to put into effect. But I should

Rules oj the House
like to have a little more definite, pronouncement that the government as a government do not accept them as a direction and do not interpret the voting of the committee on these amendments as an approval of the suggestions made in the preamble and as a direction to the government for the conduct of the business of the House of Commons. If that clarification were made there would be less difficulty in accepting or disposing of the suggested amendments.
I suggest that we need to know what is really the position and what is to become of the preamble.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: May I interrupt the hon. member. Perhaps he was not in the house when we discussed this question before, but the Chairman has ruled that it is not a preamble but a part of the report, and that makes the position worse.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
It makes my position
stronger if it is a part of the report of the committee. In dealing with it at the present time and approving the suggested amendments which we are presently discussing, we are approving that other part of the report with which so many members have expressed disagreement. That is the position I propose to take myself, and I do not hesitate to give my vote against the first amendment, having in mind that I am also opposing the suggestions that are contained in the preamble.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Several questions have been asked this evening regarding the amendment to standing order 9. One statement was that it was not contained in Doctor Beauchesne's, third edition. The reason is this. It was not transferred from the second to the third edition because of the uncertainty of the law with regard to voting in the house. When that matter was brought before the committee I perhaps insisted more than others that some declaration should be made by this committee, because after all we were dealing with the rules of the house where corrections could be made which were necessary in the light of the experience of past years and this was the time to do it. I had it brought before me in the house the week before the first meeting of the committee. There was a vote in the house, and one hon. member asked me whether a certain member who had not voted should not be compelled to vote. I stated that I preferred not to give a decision then because the law to my mind was not clear and I did not know what powers I had to compel a member to vote, and if I did endeavour to compel him I did not know what penalty I could impose upon him if he did not vote. The result was that the question has been in a state of
indecision, and it is a serious matter, because I can quite well understand that a question might be raised on some issue which was being voted upon, upon which there might be keen anxiety, and there might be considerable delay in the proceedings of the house, which might give rise to contentions that need not ensue. Consequently, when the committee considered the matter, they adopted this amendment and put it before the house. As I have already said, the committee have endeavoured as best they could to interpret what might be the wishes of the house. Hon. members have now this amendment before them and must decide what shall be the law of the house when this report is finally disposed of.
The difficulty in this matter is that if the house does not agree to the amendment, we are then placed in the same position as we were in before, with an indecisive law so far as the. house is concerned, and that, makes it rather difficult for a Speaker to enforce the law, supposing he is asked by the house to do so. The rejection of the amendment will mean, therefore, that we shall be back where we were before. I do not know how we can rectify that. I should like to see some declaration from the house either for or against, but if it is against then I think something should take its place. Either the member should be obliged to vote, or he should not be obliged to vote. If the house in its wisdom arrives at a decision in that regard, that is all I want; but speaking personally I do wish to have some direction from the house.
The hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) has referred to the introduction to the report. I have emphasized already that there was no intention on the part of the committee that the introduction should be considered as obliging either the government or the house to make amendments to the rules. These recommendations, as they are called, in the preamble were never intended to be recommendations which the government should implement; they were simply the thoughts in the mind of the committee at that time as to ways in which the procedure of the house might be altered in the discretion of the government and of the house. I think the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres is not correct when he says that the report as a whole will be reported by this committee to the house. What the chairman will report will be the amendments the committee has approved; it will not be the report itself. That is what was done in 1927. There was no long preamble then, but on March 22 of that year, at page 316 of the Journals, I find this:
The report of the special committee appointed to consider the advisability of revising the standing orders usually called the rules of the
Rules of the House

house, was again considered in committee of the whole, reported with amendments, considered as amended, and concurred in, on division, as follows.
There was no preamble, if it can be so called, to the report of that special committee, but in conclusion this is stated:
If the proposed changes are concurred in by the house, it will be necessary to renumber and reprint the rules. Your committee recommends that the present report be only put in force at the next session of parliament. All of which is respectfully submitted.
Itodolphe Lemieux,
Chairman.
The position will be that the chairman of this committee will repo'rt the amendments which have been moved and to which the concurrence of the house is desired. There is no question in my mind, and I think there can be none in the mind of any hon. member of this committee, that a government could possibly propose to found any legislation upon recommendations such as those referred to, especially in view of the expressions of opinion which have come from hon. members in opposition to the recommendations contained in the first part of the report. The house will simply concur or not concur, as the case may be, in the recommendations of the committee as far as the proposed amendments are concerned.
Personally I saw no necessity for the discussion that took place on the introductory portion of the report, because after all what the house has to deal with are the amendments that are being proposed to the rules of the house. These proposed amendments have been approved by the special committee; if reported by this committee and adopted by the house, they will form part of the rules of the house. The hon. member for New Westminster referred to a citation in connection with amending the rules of the house. Hon. members will realize that a citation in Doctor Beauchesne's book is of value in showing the practice that haS been followed in the past, and possibly in pointing out the law, but it has not the effect of a standing order. You cannot amend a citation in Doctor Beauchesne's book, but you can amend a standing order.
The hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres requested the government to make a statement with respect to the introduction to the report and the statements contained therein, to the effect that the government disagrees with it and that it will not be considered as a precedent. The fact is that this report comes from a committee of the house, not from the government. Each member of the government is only an individual member of the house as far as this report is concerned. After the discussion which has taken place

to-day, however, I am sure any future government that proposed to found any action upon the report would only have to read the pages of Hansard to know that the introduction was not considered as part of the proposed amendments to the rules.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres asked by what authority I was occupying the Chair at the present time and what sort of report would be made to the house. The authority will be seen at page 1107 of Hansard -for March 3, 1944:
Mr. Speaker:	I have the honour to present
the first and final report of the special committee appointed to assist Mr. Speaker in revising the standing orders of the house.
Hon. Ian A. Mackenzie (Minister of Pensions and National Health):	With the consent of
the house I move:
"That the report of Mr. Speaker for the special committee on the revision of the standing orders be referred to the committee of the whole on Tuesday next."

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to.
This afternoon when Mr. Speaker left the Chair and the house went into committee of the whole, after calling "order" I presented the following order to the committee: "House in committee of the whole to consider certain amendments to standing orders. Standing order 9". Then I read the amendment which is now before the committee. When I make the final report on the matter now under consideration by the committee of the whole, this will be the report to Mr. Speaker: "Mr. Speaker, the committee of the whole have adopted certain proposed amendments to the standing orders of the House of Commons, and have directed me to report the same".

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
May I draw your attention to the fact that when you are reporting to the Chair a matter which has been considered in committee of the whole, you do not report that certain amendments have been considered by the committee of the whole. You report a bill that has been considered by the committee, together with the amendments that have been made in committee of the whole. In this case your power has been given under the motion of the Prime Minister on March 7 that the house proceed to take up in committee of the whole the report made to the house by the special committee. That is what is now before this committee; that is the report we are at present considering. I submit with all due respect that when you report to the Chair your report must be, "The committee has been considering the report made by the special committee appointed to consider amendments to the standing orders of the House of Commons." If you want to make a report in accordance

Rules of the House
with the motion, you must state that the committee of the whole has considered the report of the special committee; you cannot say simply, "I am reporting certain amendments." Amendments to what? Where have you taken them from? Who proposes these amendments? You have been taking these amendments from the report of the committee, so that you must present to the Chair the report of the committee, not just the amendments, which means that you must report the preamble as well as the amendments themselves.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I must repeat that this special committee was appointed to assist Mr. Speaker in revising the standing orders of the house. The special committee reported to the house and the report was referred to the committee of the whole, to consider and pass or amend the amendments contained in the report.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: But that does not alter the fact that what we have before us is a report, with which we must deal in its entirety. You cannot separate one section from the other. We are considering the whole report, whatever it is.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, for the sake of the record may I say that, generally speaking, I am in agreement with the preamble as set out in the report. But definitely I wish to say I regard the amendment to standing order 9 as a detriment to the rights and privileges of private members of the House of Commons.
Generally speaking, issues which come before the house are so clear-cut that, after considerable debate members have enough information and knowledge to decide whether they wish to vote one way or another. But now and again it may so happen that even after debate a private member is not in a position, and does not have sufficient information upon a question to vote. Only once since I have been a member of the house has such an occasion arisen, and I should like to recall it. That was the time when the official opposition asked that certain documents be placed before the house. The documents had been before the war expenditures committee and had been seen by that committee in camera. I was not of the opinion that those particular documents should be brought before the house and published in a time of war. Therefore I could not vote with the opposition. Neither could I vote in support of the government, because I had not seen the documents. To have voted in support of the government
would have been a blind vote. Upon that occasion, knowing that if I sat here I should vote, I went outside the chamber and did not vote.
Even if this amendment passes, and if occasion should arise when Mr. Speaker must name me, may I say that I would prefer to be named by Mr. Speaker than to vote blindly upon any measure. It is possible that such a question might not arise again for years. But it is also possible that a private member might be placed in another situation of exactly the same kind. I see no reason why a private member should be forced to vote, if that member does not have sufficient information to make it possible for him to vote according to his conscience. In the instance I have indicated I could not vote unless I saw the documents in question and read them through, and had satisfied myself that they were correct or incorrect. Neither, on the other hand, could I support the idea of having this placed before the public in a time of war.
In an instance such as that I feel that if one were controlled by an amendment such as the one now before us it would be somewhat of an indignity if Mr. Speaker should have to name me, or I should have to remove myself from the chamber. Therefore I state most emphatically that I shall vote against this amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Following what has been said by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres, as to the attitude of the government, may I say to him and to the committee that, assuming that the amendment now before the committee should pass-and that is all that is before the committee, in my humble opinion-so far as the government is concerned it will not regard that as an approval of anything more than is contained in that amendment.
I wish to say further, in reply to the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres, that the committee was appointed in the first place for the purpose of assisting in revising the standing orders of the house; and the preamble which my hon. friend ties on to this particular amendment has, I submit, nothing to do with the question we are now considering. The only substantive resolution before the Chair is the resolution amending standing order 9. That stands on its own feet, and is dealt with separately from anything else.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I move:
That the word "recommend" at line twenty of the second paragraph on page 2 of the report be stricken out, and that the word "suggest" be substituted therefor.
Rules oj the House

I note that in reading my amendment Mr. Chairman has had some difficulty. In the committee we have no stenographer to which we might dictate our amendments. I realize my handwriting is hard to read, so that I can understand the trouble he has had.
The sentence now reads:
We therefore recommend that, when the yearly estimates have been brought down, one day a week be set aside for consideration of supply.
With the amendment, the sentence would read:
We therefore suggest that, when the yearly estimates have been brought down, one day a week be set aside for consideration of supply.
That amendment is important, because it is no longer a recommendation from the committee. It is just a suggestion. I hope the leader of the house will understand that I have done my best to catch the olive branch he has offered to the committee. I have showed my good1 disposition, what the Prime Minister calls good will, in making the amendment. This will put everybody in a good mood, and will bring about an early settlement of the difficulty.
I have never attended any meetings of the League of Nations at Geneva, but I have tried this peace movement, this appeasement, for , those who have been dissatisfied with the way in which the report was drafted.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Order. I must say to the hon. member for Temiscouata that his amendment is out of order.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
It may be out of order, but it is the basis of the proposed amendment. And, instead of taking out the basis of the amendment, I wanted to put a little cement in it, so that it might be in better shape than it was before. Even if my amendment is out of order, it has shown my good will.
Now, if we are about to talk about the proposed amendment, we will talk about it. How many times have I boosted parliamentary institutions in the United Kingdom! His Honour the Speaker has said that at times he has been embarrassed because we have no definite rule about the right to vote when one is sitting in the house. He has said that we have no definite law. But let us first read the first standing order of the House of Commons. It states:
In all eases not provided for hereinafter or by sessional or other orders, the usages and customs of the House of Commons of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland as in force at the time shall be followed so far as they may be applicable to this house.
[Mr. Pouliot.l
We may now turn to page 28 of Doctor Beauchesne's book published in 1927. The second part of citation 87 which appears on page 28 reads:	.
A member is not obliged to vote. S.O. 29, British H. of C.
I am very sorry to have to disagree with Mr. Speaker about the matter. If the former Speaker, the Hon. Mr. Lemieux, was embarrassed about deciding this matter during the hectic session of 1926, it w'as due to his ignoring the fact that there was a standing order at Westminster which ruled that members were not forced to vote. I remember that Ted Garland was a member of the house at that time, as were the late Mr. Woodsworth and Mr. Bourassa, and they all decided not to vote. They were handicapped to a certain extent when they were told that it was their duty to vote. They asked to be shown the standing order by virtue of which they were bound to vote, but nobody could show it to them.
It is now suggested that we should penalize an hon. member who remains in his seat during a division, who is not hypocritical enough to want to go behind the curtain when a vote is being taken and where all he needs to do is just cover part of his body. I maintain that it is the right of a member of parliament to stay at his desk and decide whether he will vote or not. A member should have the right to remain in his seat without having to run behind the curtain. This concerns the independence of parliament. A member of parliament should not be faced with the possibility of being named by Mr. Speaker, a thing that would bring shame upon him. He should not be forced to have to run behind a curtain where he can show his face but where he must keep one-half of his body hidden. It is the most ridiculous thing on earth to state that the report could be acceptable to anyone. I have my own Veasons for saying that.

Rules oj the House
I have listened to his nonsense and I never interjected in any way, shape or form. I was speaking to another hon. member in front of me, and I was certainly not lowering my dignity or the dignity of the house by interrupting such nonsense while we are at war.

speechtext: Order.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, will you please ask the hon. member to withdraw the language he has used. I rise to a question of privilege. The hon. member has no right to say that the remarks of another hon. member are nonsense. I want your ruling on that. If you rule in favour of the hon. member for Fraser Valley, then I will use the same language about him a million times.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I do not believe the statement made by the hon. member for Fraser Valley is unparliamentary.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Then I use it a million times against the hon. member for Fraser Valley.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
This debate appears to have resolved itself into what constitutes a report. I am of opinion that what is called the introduction or what has been referred to as the preamble should constitute part of the report. Hon. members should by their votes say whether or not they are in favour of that particular part of the report. If one looks in a dictionary he will see. that the definitions of "preamble" and "introduction" are much the same; they are almost synonymous terms. "Preamble" means preliminary remarks.
It states here specifically that this is the first and final report of this committee. In the report are two specific recommendations, which read in part as follows:
We therefore recommend that, when the yearly estimates have been brought down, one day a week be set aside for consideration of supply
The next recommendation-note that the term is "recommendation", not "suggestion"- is as follows:
Our recommendation is that, when there is reason to believe that debate will be protracted, parties and groups recognized in the house shall confer and make arrangements either for allotting days or laying any plan for saving time
What is the position? If we concur in certain recommendations which appear later on, there are still two substantial and important recommendations which will not have been dealt with and for which at some time or another there will have to be further standing orders provided. As far as the amendment to standing order 9 is concerned, I shall vote against it. I do not see why it
should be obligatory upon any member of this house to vote unless 'he sees fit to do so. As far as I am concerned I shall be responsible to my constituents for what action I take, whether I vote or whether I withhold my vote.
I suggest that it will be high time to oblige members of the house to vote, to make it obligatory that they vote, when the law of this country is that everybody shall be obliged to vote in a general election.
The position I take is that the report in its entirety should be discussed and concurred in, perhaps with some amendments. I am ready to assume the responsibility to my constituents as to whether I vote on any question that comes before the house. I can get away from that responsibility by absenting myself, but that is a poor way of doing it; that is a childish way of doing it. I submit that I should have a perfect right to exercise my own discretion and judgment and not have to face a certain penalty.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I am in entire concurrence with the statement of the previous speaker that the forepart of this report could be voted upon. Furthermore, I see no harm in registering the opinion of this committee upon these two recommendations. Before the dinner recess the hon. member for Comox-Alberni was urging that they be set out specifically at the conclusion of the discussion on the other recommendations. I should have liked to see the committee agree that at the conclusion of these recommendations, or at the first if you like, we record whether this committee is in favour of these recommendations or contrariwise. We should not have had the difficulty we had this afternoon. I submit that we can very well settle the amend-[DOT]ment to standing order 9 immediately. Surely we all have our minds made up on it. For my part I do not think it is very important one way or the other. I do not believe that most of the members of this committee think it or the two recommendations in the early part of the report merit all the debate we have had upon them.
I should like to make this suggestion to you, Mr. Chairman. There is no thought of applying closure or anything like that, but we have had a field day here this afternoon on these various proposals and also a sort of field day on a great many asides that some member or another would make, and we would then barge into a debate on them. I would appeal to you now, Mr. Chairman, that we agree to vote in due course on the two recommendations that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has so often brought to our attention this afternoon, and then let us dispose of the
Rules oj the House

amendment to standing order 9 right away, and see if we cannot get one step forward before the hands of the clock move on many minutes.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I was pleased to hear the minister who is leading the house say a few minutes ago that the preamble or introduction was not to be considered in this committee. I was glad of that because it contains a strange doctrine to which I do not subscribe. Paragraph 2 of the committee's report reads as follows, speaking of criticisms of this house by those outside:
These criticisms arise from opinions concerning the functions of parliament which are often based upon such misconceptions as the view that parliament is primarily a board of directors with the members oif the cabinet as its executive staff, and that members, instead of endeavouring to reconcile as much as possible all the elements of public opinion, which is difficult in our diversified country, should rigidly consider every question on its own exclusive merits Such however is not the true function of a legislative body composed of 245 members elected to discuss the management of public affairs Debates may sometimes be lengthy but they bring home to the administration the advisability or unpopularity of a particular line of policy and they must be heard because democratic government rests upon public opinion. Parliament is the assembly of representatives elected by the people where great issues are debated-
'Debated", mind you.
-or should be debated; it is not primarily a body of auditors charged with the inspection of departmental accounts. Freedom of speech is one of the inalienable privileges of members of the House of Commons.
And thus it goes on. This report by a committee of the House of Commons would reduce parliament to a debating society. Furthermore, it says:
Mr. Speaker, from the special committee appointed to assist him in revising the standing orders of the House of Commons, presented the first and final report of the said committee, which is as follows.
Then follows the introductory part of the report which we are told now is only drapery to the main report. We are told that it has no virtue. If it has no virtue, why is it there? When we had a motion made earlier in the evening to delete that part from the report it was ruled out of order. We are told by the people who support it that it has no virtue, and we are told by the minister leading the house that it is not to be considered by this committee. Why, then, should we not delete it? That is mysterious to me. I cannot subscribe to this part of the report and for that reason I shall vote against it.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I think the hon. member was slightly mistaken in his conception of what the hon. gentleman who is leading the house said a few moments ago. What he said in answer to the lady member was that passing of the amendment to standing order 9 in no way conveyed approval or concurrence in the earlier part of the report. The hon. gentleman behind me took that as meaning that that part of the report would not be considered at all. But the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres made it very clear that the report as a report must be adopted as such or rejected. I wish to compliment the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres upon the able way in which he expressed so well what I was saying much worse this afternoon.
The hon. member for Renfrew South made a very good suggestion. He said that he was not going to vote for this amendment to standing order 9. But a little difficulty arises there. I also agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, who made the best suggestion of all. He said that if these amendments are amendments-and they are-why not dispose of them for good or evil and let us get on. There is only one slight divergent point. I was impressed by the remarks made by Mr, Speaker. He said that there has been confusion in some places as to whether a man had or had not the right to vote.
I should like to make this suggestion, which ought to meet the whole situation and expedite the thing. Mr. Speaker gave the impression that he was not so deadly struck on putting through this amendment in its present form, but he did want a definite ruling by which he could govern himself in the days, and I hope years, which are to come. I therefore move the following amendment:
That all the words after the word "added" in the proposed amendment be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"A member present in the chamber when the question is finally put by Mr. Speaker shall not be obliged to vote."
That would give us a definite ruling which should satisfy the desire of Mr. Speaker for definite instructions. I think it would also meet the wishes of a large number of members, and it would also be in accordance with the rule which has prevailed in the British House of Commons for thirty-eight years. It might be said that this amendment is unnecessary, since voting against the main motion would have the same effect, but I am moving it to meet the situation envisioned by the Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Standing order 9 reads:
Upon a division, the yeas and nays shall not be entered upon the minutes, unless demanded by five members.

Rules oj the House
The special committee propose the following amendment:
And every member present in the chamber when the question is finally put iby Mr. Speaker shall be obliged to vote, and if he does not vote Mr. Speaker shall call upon him to vote and his name shall be recorded accordingly. If he persists in not voting he may be named by Mr. Speaker for having violated a standing order of the house.
Mr. Neill moves as an amendment to the amendment:
That all the words after "added" ibe struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"A member present in the chamber when the question is finally put by Mr. Speaker shall not be obliged to vote."

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Before the motion is put I should like to know what is the position of the preamble at the moment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: That matter was discussed this afternoon when we went into committee. I made a ruling, and a general discussion was allowed on the report.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Moreover, Mr. Chairman,
you ruled out an amendment to delete the preamble. There was a motion made to delete the preamble and you ruled that out. Subsequently, the minister who was leading the house said, I think, that the preamble was not being considered by the house and would not be part of the report.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: If my hon. friend is referring to the passage which I think he is referring to, it was in answer to the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres, who asked for an assurance by the government that an approval or a disposition of the amendment to standing order 9 would not be regarded as an approval of the sentiments or the recommendations or the suggestions contained in the preamble, and I made the positive statement that the passing of the amendment to standing order 9 would be regarded only as an approval of that amendment in the terms in which it was set out.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: What is the position of the preamble in the picture?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
As I see it, if I may suggest this to the committee, there is before the committee no motion with regard to the preamble at all,'but there is a definite motion before the chair that standing order 9 be amended by adding the clause which is here, and that is all that is before the committee. The committee was desirous of discussing the preamble, which contains no amendment whatever to any standing order-and I remind the committee that the special committee was appointed for the purpose of amending the
standing orders, not for the purpose of making suggestions or recommendations of the kind which are contained in the preamble-but because of the fact that this amendment is the only thing which is before this committee, and not the preamble, that is the thing which I think the committee should consider.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Do you not think that the fact that the matter has been dealt with in the way it was gives the unanimous approval of the house to the introduction?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Let me make it clear
that the government is taking no part in this. I am sitting back and watching the members of the house deal with the rules of the house, and I am taking just as little part in it as possible. I am glad to help if I can, but I have heard a good deal this afternoon about democracy, free speech, and things of that kind, and I think Hansard will show pretty good evidence that there has not been much restriction in that respect. Whether or not that has contributed to the effective consideration of the serious question which we have had to consider, namely the substantive recommendations in the committee's report, remains to be seen. However, as far as the government is concerned, hon. members have had a perfectly free rein in that respect, and all I have done is attempt to help if I could, to see that the rules of the house which we have at the present time and which are not amended are carried out, and hon. members are at liberty to make any such motions as they think proper if they are within the rules of the house. My own thought was that a motion regarding the preamble was not within the rules of the house, because a motion had been made by the Speaker and was put by the Chairman, a specific motion amending standing order 9. No motion is before the Chair at the present time with regard to the preamble, and I find it difficult to bring myself to think that by any stretch of the imagination, either the approving or disapproving of that amendment to standing order 9 can be regarded in any way as expressing any view one way or the other on what is set out in that preamble. It just means that it is disregarded, and that when these matters come up for consideration-and, by the way, one of them could be germane to a standing order of the house-they will have to come up, not by way of a recommendation such as we have here, but by way of an amendment to the standing orders. The one I have in mind could be related to standing order 17, which provides that when government business has precedence, government orders may be called in such sequence as the government may think fit. If the committee
Rules of the House

or anyone else wants to attempt to put into effect the suggestion or recommendation contained in that preamble with respect to the setting aside of special days for the discussion of estimates, he would have to bring forward and place in the hands of the Chairman a substantative amendment to standing order 17, and that has not been done. The preamble does nothing more than express some pious opinions as to what might be done, in the opinion of a committee of this house. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the situation is pretty clear. We have roamed over a great deal of ground, but we are back to just one thing; that is, must a member vote or may he not? That is all there is to it. The amendment suggested, if I may say so, is rather vague; it just says that hon. members shall not be obliged to vote. Somebody will say, "So what?" Supposing a question is put and no hon. member votes; what then?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I wonder if I may ask the hon. member for Marquette whether in his opinion this is a proper amendment.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I have no objection to the amendment personally, for reasons I have given already, though it might have the implications of an expanded negative. The amendment merely provides that a member in' the chamber at the time a vote is called shall not be obliged to register his vote. Penalties are provided in the original amendment which will be deleted if this amendment carries; and while I do think it comes somewhat near the realm of an expanded negative, yet I think it is in order. It denies the purport of the original amendment, but it adds a provision to the standing order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Those in favour of the amendment will kindly say, yea.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Yea.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Before the vote is taken-

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: The vote has been taken.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Before the vote is taken, in view of the fact that the more recent statements which have been made in the committee have been opposed-

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I maintain that the question has been put.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: On the point of order, I may have been a little hasty in calling for the vote.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: As I started to say, in view of the fact that the more recent statements made this evening on this subject have been in opposition to the idea of compulsory voting, I feel that I should briefly state my view, which is on the other side. As a matter of fact, it seems to me that if this amendment should carry, the last state would be worse than the first; then we would find ourselves with a standing order stating specifically that hon. members were not obliged to vote. My fear is that, as a result, in the future there would be more abstention from voting than there has been in the past.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: We might not have a vote at all.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
As the Minister of
Pensions and National Health interjects, there might be no vote at all. I see it in very simple terms. I was sent here by a constituency which has a population of some sixty or sixty-five thousand people. I am supposed to be a responsible person representing those people; I feel it my duty to give consideration to all matters that come to a vote in this house, and I feel I should be obliged to vote. I hope that the amendment will be defeated and that the main motion will carry.
While I am on my feet may I say that I shall oppose some of the other amendments that are to come before us just as vigorously as some hon. members are opposing this one. So far as this one is concerned, I feel that in the form in which the committee gave it to us it should be adopted.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I am still a bit puzzled as to the point of order. As I understand the position at present, this matter is before the committee as a result of the motion of the Prime Minister that the Speaker leave the Chair for the house to go into committee to consider a report from a special committee. If that is the case I ask for your ruling, Mr. Chairman. I may be wrong in this, but it would appear to me that the extent to which we can go is either to reject that portion of the report we are dealing with or to refer it back to the committee with appropriate recommendations. If my understanding of the matter is correct, this committee has no power of its own volition to amend a committee's report that is before us in the manner in which this report is before the committee. I want a ruling on that point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I did not clearly catch the point the hon. member was making. There is quite a bit of murmuring around me.

Rules oj the House

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
My point of order is this.
The particular matter we are discussing comes before the committee as a result of a motion of the Prime Minister that Mr. Speaker leave the Chair to permit us to go into committee to consider this report from a special committee. Has a member of this committee the right to do more than reject, to vote against the recommendations of that committee, or to move that the report be referred back to the committee for further consideration?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
The report could be
amended.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
This is exactly what has happened before. The hon. gentleman's question refers to the proposed subamendment to standing order 9. It is exactly the same as before, when I moved to dispense with the preamble or introduction or prologue contained in the first three pages. I was told it was not before the committee; but whether any motion is made by any member of this house, whether he is Prime Minister or a backbencher, makes no difference. The committee has the right to reshape it as it sees fit. It is the rule of the majority that governs in spite of what is said in this pamphlet-may I call it that-about the rights of minorities. I am ready to submit to the rule of the majority, the majority of this committee, and I am not bound by what has been decided by a special committee. They were appointed to report to us and they have reported to us. Are we or are we not satisfied? If we are not satisfied we have a right to tell them so. We can accept what they recommend to us or we can reject or change it. We have that right and that is done by the majority. That is why I appeal to the majority of the committee to get rid of the report, not to hear any more about it, because these changes would not improve the debates in the house, but would be a source of trouble and would deprive members of the rights they have. When I think of what the hon. gentleman has said, it is a matter of great concern to all of us at the present time. It is suggested by the subamendment that members shall not be obliged to vote. That is right. But there is something else. It is the basis of that recommendation, which is the three first pages, these invisible pages, which we cannot get rid of because they do not seem to be before us. If they are the basis of the report, then they are not only the basis of this subamendment, but they are the basis of each one of the subamendments and can be discussed on each one of the subamendments. Is it not better to get rid of it right away? To show how wrong the basis was for each one of the subsequent amendments, we might as well dispense with it
right away by unanimous consent and say that it is made clear that these three pages are not before the Chair at the present time.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: After to-day's debate, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that we leave the rules alone until the rules of Hitler are beaten.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I was going to suggest that the amendment is out of order since it is a direct negative, but in view of the fact that you have accepted it, Mr. Chairman, and said that it is in order, all I can say is that it is about as crazy an amendment as I have ever heard of, because we are sent to this house to carry on the business of the country; the business of the country is decided by the votes of the members and all that the amendment says is that although we are sent here to carry on the affairs of the nation, we need not do so when we come here.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: A reductio ad absurdum.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: What I was going to say might not be parliamentary, but we have here a good demonstration of about as nice a filibuster as I have seen in a long time to prevent anything being done.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: I feel it would be my duty to vote against this amendment. We have frowned upon the apathy of the public in not registering their votes, and it would be a good example to the public if they could say that even members of parliament are not obliged to vote. In consequence of that I am going to vote against the amendment.

o'clock.
Progress reported.
